kz_ikiikitei_omicho_ten.gf_detail: This is a market seafood-bowl and sushi counter. Sushi rice is seasoned with rice vinegar and the bowls are served with soy sauce, which in Japan is virtually always brewed with wheat. There is no gluten-free menu or any documented allergen accommodation, and the cramped 10-seat counter shares all prep surfaces. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_ikiikitei_omicho_ten.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built around raw fish delivered from Kanazawa Port (seafood bowls and nigiri sushi). There are no vegan or vegetarian options documented, and even the rice is served as part of seafood dishes. Not a viable choice for vegans or vegetarians.
kz_ikiikitei_omicho_ten.hours_raw: 7:00-15:00 (closes earlier when the day's fish sells out). Closed Tuesdays (Wednesday instead if Monday is a public holiday); may also close when seas are rough.
kz_ikiikitei_omicho_ten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny counter inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, いきいき亭 has become one of the market's most beloved seafood-bowl stops, opening at 7am so visitors and locals alike can start the day with fish delivered straight from Kanazawa Port. With only about ten counter seats, the cra

chef_bio.background: A tiny counter inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, いきいき亭 has become one of the market's most beloved seafood-bowl stops, opening at 7am so visitors and locals alike can start the day with fish delivered straight from Kanazawa Port. With only about ten counter seats, the cramped space naturally turns strangers into companions over a meal.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fresh fish straight from Kanazawa Port, served simply and affordably in a friendly, no-fuss market setting that's easy for solo diners to enter.
chef_bio.specialty: Signature kaisendon (seafood rice bowls) loaded with fresh local catch, including the popular Ikiikitei-don and the Tokusen Hokuriku-don (around 2,500 yen) and a smaller Mini Kanazawa-don (around 1,200 yen), plus per-plate nigiri sushi. In the Ikiikitei-don the fish toppings and the rice are served in separate vessels so you can eat them apart or combined.

anecdotes.text: Rather than queuing, diners write their name and a phone number on an order slip on the glass door; staff call when a seat opens, so you can wander the market while you wait.
The Ikiikitei-don serves the sashimi toppings and the sushi rice in separate containers, letting diners combine them to taste — part of the lively market atmosphere.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 近江町市場内、カウンター約10席の小さな海鮮丼店。朝7時開店、金沢港直送の鮮魚。特選北陸丼約2,500円、ミニ金沢丼約1,200円、握りは皿で計算。ガラス戸の紙に名前と電話番号を記入し呼ばれる方式。いきいき亭丼はネタとシャリを別容器で提供。

gf_cross_contamination.text: A roughly 10-seat market counter doing sushi and raw-fish bowls, with shared prep surfaces and no documented allergen separation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Seafood bowls and nigiri are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which is brewed with wheat; sushi rice is also vinegar-seasoned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The whole menu is fish-based (Kanazawa Port seafood bowls and sushi), with no vegan or vegetarian dishes offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, solo-friendly market counter where you write your order on a slip; a few words of Japanese help, but pointing at the popular bowls works fine for a foreign student.

kz_kaiten_sushi_okura.gf_detail: Traditional sushi counter relying on wheat-based soy sauce and seasoned sushi rice; no gluten-free accommodations are documented and cross-contact is unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kz_kaiten_sushi_okura.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused sushi restaurant built around fresh local fish, shellfish, shrimp and crab. No vegan menu or plant-based options are documented.
kz_kaiten_sushi_okura.hours_raw: 10:30-18:00 (last entry 17:30); a midday pause may occur ~15:00-17:30. Closed Wednesdays. Some sources list weekend hours extending to 19:00.
kz_kaiten_sushi_okura.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running conveyor-belt sushi shop tucked into Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, the city's kitchen. Founded around 1969 (roughly 45-50 years before its June 2024 renewal), it has been a local favorite for decades and is often named among the best kaiten-zushi in the market

chef_bio.background: A long-running conveyor-belt sushi shop tucked into Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, the city's kitchen. The shop bills itself 創業50余年 — in business for over half a century — and has been a local favorite for decades, often named among the best kaiten-zushi in the market and the city. It reopened in June 2024 after a renewal.
chef_bio.philosophy: The master's stated policy is to personally buy and hand-pick the best ingredients every morning at the market, offering only fish he has judged with his own eye — so the flavors can be found nowhere else (毎朝大将自ら市場で仕入れる).
chef_bio.specialty: Local Hokuriku seafood served over a U-shaped counter: seasonal catches such as winter kanpachi, snow crab and cod, spring firefly squid and white shrimp, plus prized gasu-ebi (a sweeter local shrimp), sweet shrimp, and traditional Kanazawa kombu-jime (kelp-cured fish).

anecdotes.text: Every morning the owner-chef himself goes into Omicho Market to source the day's fish, picking each item by expert eye rather than ordering wholesale (大将自らが毎日仕入れをし、目利きした良いものを提供するというポリシー).

Though it runs a conveyor belt, regulars order directly from the chef and watch their sushi made fresh, making it feel more like a traditional sushi bar; one local reviewer ranks it among Kanazawa's top three kaiten-zushi.
The shop reopened on 17 June 2024 after a renewal that refreshed its U-shaped counter while keeping its old-school paper-slip ordering.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイトは『創業50余年 地元に愛される老舗』とうたう近江町市場の回転寿司。U字カウンター（約20〜25席）。2024年6月17日リニューアルオープン。大将が毎朝自ら仕入れ・目利き。地物中心（がすえび・甘えび・昆布締めなど）。紙の注文票方式。

gf_cross_contamination.text: A traditional sushi counter where wheat-based soy sauce and seasoned sushi rice are used throughout; cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable and no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is the default condiment at the sushi counter.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All preparation centers on raw fish and shellfish at a shared sushi counter; any non-seafood item would share surfaces and tools with seafood.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, casual counter sushi spot inside Omicho Market where ordering is done by paper slip; basic Japanese helps but pointing and a friendly konnichiwa will get you a warm welcome.

kz_oden_takasago.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The defining dashi is built on dark soy sauce (wheat-containing) and bonito, classic ingredients include kuruma-fu (wheat gluten), and a ginger-miso topping is used. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
kz_oden_takasago.vegan_detail: A seafood-forward oden and izakaya house. The broth is a continuously replenished katsuo (bonito) and dark-soy dashi simmered with meat and fish, and signature items include beef tendon, crab, whelk and dote-yaki. No documented vegan menu, and even vegetable items share the animal-based pot.
kz_oden_takasago.hours_raw: 16:00-21:00 (may vary with how busy it is)
kz_oden_takasago.notes: [Mom & Pop] Oden Takasago has been simmering its pot in Kanazawa's Katamachi district since 1936 (Showa 11), making it one of the city's long-standing old-guard oden houses. It has stayed in the same neighborhood, and its ivy-draped exterior, red lanterns and noren curtains give it an unmist

chef_bio.background: Oden Takasago has been simmering its pot in Kanazawa's Katamachi district since 1936 (Showa 11), making it one of the city's long-standing old-guard oden houses. Its founder had grown fond of Kanto-style oden while driving a taxi in Tokyo, which shaped the shop's unusually dark, rich dashi. Its ivy-draped exterior, red lanterns and noren curtains give it an unmistakably nostalgic Showa atmosphere.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep the founding broth alive by continuously replenishing it (tsugitashi), preserving a consistent, gently rich flavor across the decades.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa oden in an unusually Kanto-style, darker and richer dashi — a continuously replenished broth topped up since the shop's founding. The slow-braised, melt-in-the-mouth beef tendon (gyusuji), skewered and served with the house's secret ginger-miso, is its signature. Other draws include seasonal kani-men (snow-crab oden, roughly November to December), whelk (baigai), kuruma-fu, akamaki and Kaga vegetables, plus less-common dishes like dote-yaki and curry oden. The ginger white-miso is also brushed over items such as daikon and tsumire.

anecdotes.text: The broth has been continuously topped up (tsugitashi) since the shop opened in 1936, giving it a deep, slightly rich Kanto-style character locals have loved for generations.
The beef tendon is braised so long it nearly melts in the mouth and is eaten with the house's secret ginger-miso, which is also applied to daikon and tsumire.
The proprietor can look stern at first but proves warm and gracious, in a space full of Showa nostalgia with an ivy-covered facade and red lanterns.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 創業昭和11年（片町）の金沢おでん老舗。創業者が東京でのタクシー運転手時代に馴染んだ関東風の濃い出汁を創業以来継ぎ足して使用。ほどける牛すじを店秘伝の生姜味噌で。大根・つみれにも生姜味噌。カニ面（11〜12月）、バイ貝・車麩・赤巻き・加賀野菜、どて焼き・カレーおでんも。蔦の外観と赤提灯の昭和情緒。

gf_cross_contamination.text: All ingredients share one communal oden pot built on a wheat-soy and bonito broth, so cross-contact is unavoidable for gluten-free or vegan diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature dashi is made with dark soy sauce (koikuchi), which contains wheat, simmered with bonito.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is simmered with meat (beef tendon) and seafood; vegetable items such as daikon and Kaga vegetables are cooked in the same animal-based pot.

cultural_comfort.note: A cash-only, Showa-era counter oden shop where little or no English is likely, so some basic Japanese and a friendly, open attitude will help a foreign student feel welcome.

kz_higashiyama_mizuho.gf_detail: This is a traditional Japanese / Kaga-cuisine eatery built around dashi, soy sauce, and pickled/cured seafood (ikura shoyu-zuke, konka mackerel, koji-zuke). Wheat-based soy sauce and dashi are central to the menu and there is no documented gluten-free handling, so it is not celiac-safe. A traveler avoiding gluten would need to ask in detail and should not assume safety.
kz_higashiyama_mizuho.vegan_detail: The set meals are centered on fish, salmon roe, nodoguro, and other seafood, with dashi-based soups. No vegan or vegetarian set is documented. This is not a suitable destination for vegans.
kz_higashiyama_mizuho.hours_raw: Mon & Fri 11:00-14:00; Tue-Thu 11:00-20:00; Sat/Sun/holidays 11:00-15:00. (Tabelog lists Tue-Thu closing as 21:00; official site lists 20:00 — hours_week uses the official 20:00.)
kz_higashiyama_mizuho.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small home-style Japanese eatery tucked into the Higashi Chaya District across from Sugawara Shrine, run by owner Takano Sachi, who carries on the hospitality her grandmother modeled.

chef_bio.origin: Higashiyama, Kanazawa — in the heart of the historic Higashi Chaya teahouse district.
chef_bio.background: A small home-style Japanese eatery tucked into the Higashi Chaya District near Sugawara Shrine, run by owner Takano Sachi, who carries on the hospitality her grandmother modeled.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner inherited her grandmother's belief that real hospitality is in genuine care rather than show — captured in the grandmother's words 'なんもないけど、ご飯食べて行きまっし！' ("Nothing fancy, but please come in and eat") and the idea that what truly matters is invisible.
chef_bio.specialty: Generous 'one soup, many sides' set meals built around local Ishikawa ingredients — a soup with several small dishes, plus a nodoguro (rosy seabass) set, served with carefully chosen Noto-area rice grown in Suzu (Koshihikari, Hitomebore, Hyakumangoku and other varieties) and local sake. Signature small plates include ikura shoyu-zuke (soy-marinated salmon roe), dried nodoguro, firefly squid pickles, and squid koji-zuke.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's spirit traces back to the owner's grandmother, who would invite people in with 'なんもないけど、ご飯食べて行きまっし！' — a humble Kanazawa-dialect welcome that became the shop's guiding ethos.
Rice is taken seriously here: diners can choose among several Ishikawa varieties grown in Suzu on the Noto Peninsula, including Koshihikari, Hitomebore and Hyakumangoku.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 東山（東茶屋街・菅原神社近く）の家庭的な和食店。店主は髙野幸で、祖母の『なんもないけど、ご飯食べて行きまっし！』のもてなしを受け継ぐ。一汁多菜の定食やのどぐろ膳、珠洲産の米（コシヒカリ・ひとめぼれ・ひゃくまん穀など）と地酒。いくら醤油漬け・干しのどぐろ・ホタルイカ漬け・いか麹漬けなどの小鉢。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu relies on soy sauce, dashi, and cured/pickled seafood; no gluten-free accommodation is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy-marinated dishes such as ikura shoyu-zuke are signature items, indicating standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce is used.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Set meals and small plates are seafood- and dashi-based; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small family-run local spot with no documented English support, so a foreign student should be ready to order in Japanese or point at the set menu.

kz_farment_cafe.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented anywhere. The vegan offerings center on wheat-based noodle dishes (green curry noodles, tantanmen/担々麺) and the cafe serves cakes, tiramisu and other wheat-flour sweets, so the kitchen handles wheat heavily. There is no mention of dedicated gluten-free preparation, a dedicated fryer, or celiac accommodation. Not safe for celiacs; gluten-free travelers should assume cross-contamination and ask directly.
kz_farment_cafe.vegan_detail: This is a vegan-friendly omnivore cafe, not a fully vegan venue. It offers a genuine and well-regarded vegan line — spicy keema curry (vegan, topped with fried onion), green curry noodles, taco rice, and a vegan tantanmen (担々麺) — explicitly described as satisfying despite containing no meat. However, much of the menu is not vegan: the signature "ultimate cheesecake" is layered baked-and-cream cheesecake topped with grated Parmesan, and there are dairy lattes, tiramisu and other non-vegan sweets. Vegans can eat well from the savory curry/noodle items but should confirm each dish.
kz_farment_cafe.notes: fArment Cafe opened in December 2020 in Otomaru-machi, a quiet pocket of eastern Kanazawa near Higashi-Kanazawa Station. chef_bio.background: fArment Cafe opened in December 2020 in Otomaru-machi, a quiet pocket of eastern Kanazawa near Higashi-Kanazawa Station. Owner Suzuki began not with a storefront but with a mobile coffee cart called 'madera campana,' and the fixed cafe grew out of that love of coffee. The space is a renovated roadside garage/warehouse, reimagined with high ceilings, moody lighting, mismatched sofas and curated art into what the owner wanted to be 'a cafe unlike anywhere else in Kanazawa' — a sophisticated hideaway that feels like the set of a foreign film.
chef_bio.philosophy: Coffee-first craft (roasting and hand-drip done in-house) paired with an unhurried, welcoming atmosphere; the cafe is also dog-friendly, drawing friends catching up, remote workers and casual meetings alike.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-roasted specialty coffee is the heart of the shop: beans from various single origins are roasted in-house on a large roaster in the corner and hand-dripped to order, alongside playful drinks like tiramisu and prune lattes. The signature dessert is an 'ultimate cheesecake' that layers baked and cream cheesecake and finishes with a cheese-cream top and grated Parmesan. The food side is known for its vegan-friendly cooking — a spicy vegan keema curry crowned with crisp fried onions, green curry noodles, taco rice and a vegan tantanmen — plus seasonal treats like a Korean-style 'pinsu' shaved-ice dessert.

anecdotes.text: Owner Suzuki started out running a mobile coffee cart named 'madera campana' before opening the brick-and-mortar fArment Cafe, which still roasts its own beans in-house.
The cafe is set inside a renovated roadside garage/warehouse with American-industrial styling and an assortment of distinct sofas, and it welcomes dogs indoors.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Manpuku-Kanazawa articles and the Tabelog listing confirm the Dec 15 2020 opening in Otomaru, owner Suzuki's 'madera campana' cart origin, the renovated garage/warehouse interior with varied sofas and dog-friendly policy, in-house roasting, and the vegan keema curry, green-curry noodles, taco rice, vegan tantanmen, prune/tiramisu lattes, parmesan cheesecake and pinsu shaved ice.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu is wheat-heavy (noodle-based vegan curries, tantanmen, cakes and tiramisu), so a shared kitchen handling flour and noodles is expected. No gluten-free precautions are documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a mixed vegan / non-vegan kitchen. The signature cheesecake is topped with Parmesan and dairy lattes are served, so vegan dishes are prepared in a kitchen that also handles cheese and dairy; no separate vegan prep is documented.

positives.text: Offers a genuine, well-liked vegan menu (spicy vegan keema curry, green curry noodles, taco rice, vegan tantanmen) described as satisfying despite containing no meat.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, stylish hideaway cafe where a foreign student can comfortably linger over coffee and a vegan curry; staff likely operate mainly in Japanese, so a few basic phrases help, but the casual menu and counter make it easy.

kz_omicho_shokudo.gf_detail: This is a seafood izakaya whose menu centers on sashimi and seafood rice bowls (served with wheat-based soy sauce), tempura, and breaded tonkatsu — all of which contain or are dipped in gluten. Japanese dashi and seasonings here typically contain wheat-derived soy sauce. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or allergen handling is documented. Not suitable for celiacs or anyone needing strict gluten avoidance.
kz_omicho_shokudo.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused restaurant built around fresh fish bought daily at Omicho Market — signature dishes are seafood rice bowls, sashimi, and nodoguro. Stocks and broths are fish/dashi based and there is no documented vegan or vegetarian menu. Not a viable choice for vegans or vegetarians.
kz_omicho_shokudo.notes: Omicho Shokudo has operated inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market since its founding in 1930 (Showa 5), making it a roughly 95-year-old market institution. It sits right where locals and visitors come to eat the morning's catch.

chef_bio.background: Omicho Shokudo has operated inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market since its founding in 1930 (Showa 5), making it a roughly 95-year-old market institution. It sits right where locals and visitors come to eat the morning's catch, steps from the market's Emza entrance.
chef_bio.philosophy: A founding principle that has never changed: the proprietor personally inspects and buys the fish, shellfish, and vegetables every morning, serving 'delicious food in generous portions' from ingredients sourced daily within the market.
chef_bio.specialty: Seafood rice bowls (kaisendon) are the long-standing No.1 dish, served since the founding; the kitchen is also known for sashimi platters and boat-style assortments, tempura, and freshly fried tonkatsu — plus seasonal Hokuriku fish such as nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) — alongside local sake and craft beer, and it doubles as an izakaya.

anecdotes.text: The signature kaisendon (seafood rice bowl) has been the restaurant's most popular dish ever since it opened in 1930.
The owner hand-picks each morning's fish and produce in Omicho Market himself, a practice kept up since the founding.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site states the 1930 (Showa 5) founding, the unchanged practice of the owner buying fish and vegetables every morning, the motto of serving delicious food in generous portions, and kaisendon as the signature alongside sashimi, tempura and tonkatsu; it does not single out nodoguro, so that fish is hedged as a seasonal offering.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu is built on sashimi, tempura, and tonkatsu; tempura and tonkatsu are wheat-battered/breaded and fried, with high cross-contamination risk for shared fryers.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sashimi and seafood bowls are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which is wheat-based; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen is centered on fish and seafood prepared daily; broths and dishes are dashi/fish based with no documented vegan preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, long-running market eatery where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the picture menu will get you a great seafood bowl; staff are used to tourists but English may be limited.

kz_kanazawa_oden_ippukuya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. This is a Kanazawa oden shop whose dashi is soy-sauce/salt based and whose menu is built around wheat-containing items — the signature 車麩 (kuruma-fu) is literally wheat gluten, and fish cakes, atsuage and ganmodoki also typically contain wheat. All items simmer in a shared communal dashi pot, so cross-contamination is unavoidable. No dedicated gluten-free preparation.
kz_kanazawa_oden_ippukuya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The communal oden broth is a kombu-and-salt/soy dashi that almost certainly includes fish-derived dashi typical of Kanazawa oden, and the pot also simmers seafood (ばい貝 bay shellfish, fish cakes, のど黒/えび seafood items) and beef tendon. Plant items such as tofu, atsuage, ganmodoki, daikon and 車麩 exist but are cooked in the shared animal-based broth, so they are not vegan.
kz_kanazawa_oden_ippukuya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ippukuya is a Kanazawa-oden stall set inside Ippuku Yokocho, a small food-court alley in the heart of Omicho Market, Kanazawa's centuries-old central market. The yokocho gathers a handful of stalls — Ippukuya for oden, a seafood grill stand, and a local-sake counter — under a sha

chef_bio.background: Ippukuya is a Kanazawa-oden stall set inside Ippuku Yokocho, a small food-court alley in the heart of Omicho Market, Kanazawa's centuries-old central market. The yokocho gathers a handful of stalls — Ippukuya for oden, a seafood/hamayaki grill stand, and a local-sake counter — under a shared eat-in space where you take a seat first and then order at each counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built around the market itself — tofu items (yakidofu, atsuage, ganmodoki) come from the neighboring Tofuya Shibata and fish cakes from market kamaboko makers, so the oden showcases the produce of the surrounding stalls.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa-style oden simmered in a gentle kombu-and-salt dashi. Signature and seasonal items include 車麩 (kuruma-fu, broth-soaked wheat gluten), ばい貝 (bay shellfish), and the local luxury 'men' pieces — のど黒面 (nodoguro), えび面 (shrimp) and the winter かに面 (crab) — alongside everyday oden like daikon, egg, atsuage, ganmodoki, octopus and beef tendon.

anecdotes.text: A 2026 visitor described the kuruma-fu as soaking up the broth into a juicy bite and the bay shellfish as large and crunchy with natural umami, and finished by mixing leftover local sake with the oden broth for a 'dashi-sake' nightcap.
The stall sources its tofu items from Tofuya Shibata within the market and offers premium seasonal pieces such as nodoguro-men and a winter crab-men.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Onarimon's tasting report and the Kachigumi menu confirm the kombu-salt dashi, kuruma-fu and large crunchy bay shellfish, the dashi-sake finish, the food-court layout of Ippuku Yokocho, Tofuya Shibata as the tofu supplier, and the premium nodoguro-men (¥1,500) and winter-limited crab-men (¥2,300).

gf_cross_contamination.text: All oden items are simmered together in one shared dashi pot, and the broth and many items (fish cakes, the signature wheat-gluten 車麩) contain wheat/gluten, so cross-contamination is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kanazawa oden dashi is a salt/soy-sauce-seasoned kombu broth; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: FALSE WARNING. The only person who has actually tasted and described this broth calls it 昆布から取った出汁の塩ベースのスープ — kombu dashi on a SALT base — and never mentions 醤油. The claim asserts soy-sauce seasoning the source contradicts. The real gluten at いっぷくや is solid, not liquid: 車麩, ebiten/goboten tempura an

vegan_cross_contact.text: Plant items (tofu, atsuage, daikon, 車麩) are cooked in the same broth as seafood (bay shellfish, fish cakes) and beef tendon and in a likely fish-based dashi, so they are not free of animal contact.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 「金沢おでんを食べてみた(くるまふ、ばい貝、赤巻、ふかし、厚揚げ、牛すじ)」／「バイ貝(梅貝)。大きくてコリコリした食感に貝の旨味が出ていてそこにお出汁。」／「厚揚げ。大きくて出汁つゆをよく吸ってくれて美味しい！」 Tofu and daikon come from the official menu instead: 'Yakidofu(Specially made by Tofuya Shibata) 250yen', 'Atsuage … 300yen', 'Daikon 300yen', 'Konnyaku 200yen', 'Gyusuji kushi 300yen'.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual market food-court stall where you grab a seat first, then point at the oden items you want at the counter — very approachable for a foreign student with only a few words of Japanese, though menus and staff are mostly Japanese.

kz_kanazawaya_coffee_ten_om.gf_detail: This is a coffee shop, not a gluten-free destination. Coffee and espresso drinks are naturally gluten-free, but the cafe also serves cakes and sweets and makes no gluten-free claims; there is no dedicated handling and a celiac traveler cannot rely on any safety measures here.

chef_bio.background: 金澤屋珈琲店 is a long-established Kanazawa coffee specialist whose flagship sits right beside Kanazawa Castle's Kuromon gate, overlooking the Otemon moat from a traditional machiya townhouse. This branch carries that roaster into the heart of Omicho Market, the city's centuries-old 'kitchen,' at the Jukkenmachi (十間町) entrance, serving freshly hand-dripped coffee to market shoppers and travelers.
chef_bio.philosophy: The company roasts its own beans and emphasizes carefully, individually hand-brewed coffee meant to reflect Kanazawa's culture and seasons; the flagship received the 35th Kanazawa Urban Beauty and Culture Award (2012).
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-dripped self-roasted coffee, the house Omicho Blend, espresso drinks, and a Kanazawa-style gold-leaf soft serve.

anecdotes.text: The parent shop is celebrated for brewing each cup one at a time through its own net filter in a townhouse with moat views beside Kanazawa Castle, and was honored with the 35th Kanazawa Urban Beauty and Culture Award.

Inside Omicho Market this branch, at the Jukkenmachi entrance, is known for freshly brewed coffee dripped in view of customers, the house Omicho Blend, and a gold-leaf soft serve, a nod to Kanazawa's famous gold leaf.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Kanazawa tourism site describes the flagship beside the castle's Kuromon gate, its net-filter one-cup drip and self-roasting; the 35th (FY2012) Kanazawa Urban Beauty & Culture Award is confirmed by the city award records; and the Tabelog page for the Omicho branch confirms its Jukkenmachi location, the 近江町ブレンド (Omicho Blend), visible hand-dripping and the gold-leaf soft serve.

chef_bio.background: A lively, easy-to-enter conveyor-belt sushi house set right inside Kanazawa's Omicho Market, the city's centuries-old 'kitchen.' Its location means the fish travels only steps from the market stalls to the counter, and the room draws a cross-section of locals and visitors of every age, from grandparents to small children.
chef_bio.philosophy: An approachable, casual take on sushi: the shop describes itself as a spirited, welcoming place built for everyday enjoyment rather than formal fine dining.
chef_bio.specialty: Local Hokuriku seafood served as nigiri off the rotating belt and as generous kaisendon (seafood rice bowls) — including prized regional catches like nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) and sweet shrimp (amaebi).

anecdotes.text: The shop sits inside Omicho Market near the produce-street entrance, prizing freshness from its market location.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site and its About page confirm the Omicho-Market conveyor-belt sushi format, the lively/easy-to-enter self-description spanning all ages, 2009 television coverage across Nagoya/Osaka/Ishikawa and appearances in Mapple and Rurubu guides, and a kaisendon-plus-nigiri menu of local seafood.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Conveyor-belt sushi setting with shared belts, soy sauce dispensers, and prep surfaces makes cross-contact with wheat highly likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) is the default condiment for nigiri and donburi here; no wheat-free tamari is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is seafood-centric with shared rice and surfaces; no vegan preparation is documented and cross-contact with fish is unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A lively, welcoming conveyor-belt sushi spot inside the market where you can point at plates or photos, so a foreign student gets by easily with a friendly konnichiwa and a few gestures.

chef_bio.background: LOVE for ALL opened on March 21, 2023 in Kanazawa's central Korinbo district — taking over the space that formerly housed Oriental Brewing's Korinbo location — bringing a Los Angeles-born, health-conscious dining concept to one of Japan's great food cities. It is the sister restaurant of Shojin, a well-known Japanese restaurant in Los Angeles run by the owner's twin brother, which specializes in authentic Japanese cooking for the health-conscious market. The owner saw that Kanazawa's abundance of fresh produce and rich culinary heritage was the perfect foundation for a restaurant blending organic, plant-based cuisine with local tradition.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen's motto centers on connection -- with others, with family and friends -- and on serving 'real food.' Everything is handmade from scratch with carefully chosen organic ingredients, avoiding chemical preservatives, artificial colors, chemical seasonings, and refined sugar, while accommodating gluten-free, vegan, vegetarian, soy-free, onion-free, and garlic-free needs so that, as the owner puts it, more people can dine with peace of mind.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based reinterpretations of Kanazawa's iconic comfort foods: a vegan burger built on a Kaga lotus-root patty with a gluten-free bun and plant-based cheese; a vegan Hanton rice (the city's signature omelet-rice dish, adapted without meat or wheat); an oil-fried-tofu-base pizza with vegan cheese; and a cucumber 'sashimi' presented like fatty tuna using summer Kaga vegetables.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant is the sister establishment of Shojin in Los Angeles, run by the owner's twin brother, and was created to expand the joy of eating and become a place where more people can come with peace of mind.
It opened on March 21, 2023, taking over the central Korinbo space that formerly housed Oriental Brewing's Korinbo location.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kanazawa-tsu, the official loveforall-kanazawa.com site and Kanazawa Days confirm the March 21 2023 opening in Korinbo (former Oriental Brewing Korinbo location), the Shojin-LA twin-brother connection, the 'Real Food / Connection' philosophy with no chemical preservatives, artificial colour, chemical seasonings or refined sugar, the GF/vegan/vegetarian/soy-/onion-/garlic-free accommodations, and dishes including the lotus-root vegan burger, meat-and-wheat-free Hanton rice, tofu-crust pizza and cucumber toro sashimi.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant accommodates a wide range of dietary needs including gluten-free, vegan, vegetarian, soy-free, onion-free, and garlic-free, and all dishes are handmade from scratch with carefully selected ingredients.

No dedicated gluten-free kitchen, fryer, or cross-contamination protocol is documented, so celiac travelers should confirm in person and stick to the rice-flour sweets and naturally GF items rather than the pita-based dishes.
kz_siu_coffee_veg_shiu_coff.vegan_detail: Fully plant-based cafe. The entire menu is vegan: falafel sandwich (chickpea croquettes with vegetables in pita), hummus, rice-flour gateau chocolate with sweet-potato-and-cashew cream, ginger sodas, and oat-milk-based coffee ("Oats Brew"). The owner describes living plant-based herself and built the cafe around sharing those benefits, so vegan diners can order anything on the menu.

chef_bio.background: SIU.COFFEE +VEG opened on April 24, 2025 in central Kanazawa's Sachimachi district, inside a roughly 100-year-old machiya (traditional wooden townhouse) that previously housed a restaurant and was restored over about seven months. The renovation preserved the original wooden beams and lofty vaulted ceilings and added skylights, with the interior softened by herbs and wild plants and a garden view from the roughly 16 seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: Owner Kanako Mizutaka built the cafe around a 'Love yourself' concept and a wish to provide 'the safest possible meals in Ishikawa,' wanting to share the physical and emotional benefits she has experienced through plant-based living and to offer a calm refuge where busy people can reconnect with themselves.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan Middle Eastern fare: the signature falafel sandwich (chickpea croquettes with vegetables and hummus in pita), hummus, and a rice-flour gateau chocolate with sweet-potato-and-cashew cream sourced from atelier 絲 in the Kaga/Kahoku area. Drinks include house-made ginger syrup sodas and an oat-milk 'Oats Brew' coffee.

anecdotes.text: Owner Kanako Mizutaka said she wants to share the physical and emotional benefits she has experienced through plant-based living, running the space under a 'Love yourself' concept as a refuge for busy people.
The century-old townhouse underwent about seven months of restoration that kept its wooden beams and vaulted ceiling, with the cafe seating overlooking a garden.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kanazawa Keizai Shimbun and Food Japon confirm the April 24 2025 opening in Sachimachi, owner Kanako Mizutaka, the ~100-year machiya restored over ~7 months with preserved beams/vaulted ceiling and skylights, the 16-seat garden-view room, the 'Love yourself' concept, and the falafel sandwich, hummus, ginger-syrup sodas, oat-milk coffee and Kaga-sourced rice-flour gateau chocolat.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based pita bread is central to the falafel sandwich and is served alongside hummus, so wheat is handled in the kitchen and the menu is not celiac-safe despite some rice-flour sweets being available.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The cafe is fully plant-based, so there is no animal-product cross-contact risk across the menu.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner states a mission to provide 'the safest possible meals in Ishikawa,' indicating attention to ingredient safety, though no specific allergen or cross-contamination protocol is documented.

positives.text: Entirely vegan menu, so all dishes are free of meat, fish, dairy and egg.
Offers genuinely gluten-free rice-flour (米粉) sweets — a gateau chocolate made with rice rather than wheat flour — for diners avoiding gluten.
Uses oat milk for coffee and house-made ginger syrup, supporting dairy-free ordering.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, internationally-minded vegan cafe whose menu (falafel, hummus, oat-milk coffee) is familiar to foreign students; a few words of Japanese or pointing at the menu will be plenty, and the staff are used to health-conscious and overseas visitors.

kz_kenkoshoku_kobo_takano.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The kitchen cooks with traditional Japanese seasonings including soy sauce (typically wheat-based) and miso, and the official site explicitly states wheat and soy sauce are among allergens used and that there is no gluten-free menu. The signature sprouted/activated brown rice is naturally GF, but dishes overall are not celiac-safe. Guests with severe allergies are asked to inquire in advance.
kz_kenkoshoku_kobo_takano.vegan_detail: Fully plant-based. The restaurant cooks entirely without animal products — no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy — and also avoids white sugar and chemical additives. Macrobiotic and shojin-style natural cuisine built around sprouted/activated brown rice (発芽活性玄米) and seasonal vegetables, served as a chef's-choice set menu.
kz_kenkoshoku_kobo_takano.hours_raw: 11:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:00), Monday-Saturday. May close earlier if the day's food sells out.
kz_kenkoshoku_kobo_takano.notes: A small natural-food restaurant in Kanazawa run single-handedly by its owner, open since 2000 (more than two decades). It grew out of a simple wish: to create a place where you can eat food that is genuinely delicious while caring for both your body and the earth.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa, Ishikawa — in the 三口新町 area toward Nomachi and the Teramachi temple district.
chef_bio.background: A small natural-food restaurant in Kanazawa run single-handedly by its owner, open since 2000 (more than two decades). It grew out of a simple wish: to create a place where you can eat food that is genuinely delicious while caring for both your body and the earth.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything is cooked without white sugar, animal products (meat, fish, eggs, dairy), or chemical additives, using purified water, with the aim of serving the blessings of nature in as natural a state as possible. The owner sees food choices as directly connected to personal wellbeing and the health of the planet.
chef_bio.specialty: Chef's-choice macrobiotic set centered on sprouted activated brown rice and seasonal vegetables; additive-free bento and vegan osechi.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant has served its plant-based, additive-free cuisine continuously since 2000, run by a single owner, and frames its mission as letting guests 'eat delicious food while caring for your body and the earth.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own pages confirm the 2000 opening, single-owner operation, cooking without white sugar, animal products or chemical additives and using purified water, the chef's-choice macrobiotic set built on sprouted brown rice, vegan osechi, and the mission of eating delicious food while caring for body and earth.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat and soy sauce are listed among allergens used in the kitchen, and there is no gluten-free menu; the food is not celiac-safe.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The kitchen cooks with traditional seasonings including soy sauce, salt, and miso — soy sauce is typically wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is plant-based — no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy are used anywhere — so vegan cross-contact risk is minimal.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Guests with severe allergies are advised to inquire in advance before ordering.

positives.text: Completely plant-based cooking with no animal products, white sugar, or chemical additives, using purified water.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run natural-food spot where service is in Japanese only and there is no à la carte menu (chef's-choice set), so a foreign student is best off arriving prepared, perhaps with a translation app or a few key phrases, and asking about allergens up front.

kz_yamasan_sushi_honten.gf_detail: This is a traditional sushi and kaisen-don shop. Sushi rice is seasoned with vinegar and the bowls are served with wheat-based Japanese soy sauce; no gluten-free accommodation or separate preparation is documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_yamasan_sushi_honten.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused sushi and raw-fish kaisen-don specialist. Essentially all signature dishes are fish-based and dashi/soy are used throughout; there is no documented vegan offering.
kz_yamasan_sushi_honten.hours_raw: 9:00-16:00 (closes when ingredients run out). Open daily.
kz_yamasan_sushi_honten.notes: Yamasan Sushi is a long-established sushi house inside Kanazawa's lively Omicho Market, proud of more than 60 years of history. It sits in the heart of the market that has fed Kanazawa for centuries, and draws steady lines of visitors come for fresh local fish.

chef_bio.background: Yamasan Sushi is a long-established sushi house inside Kanazawa's lively Omicho Market, proud of more than 60 years of history. It sits in the heart of the market that has fed Kanazawa for centuries, and draws steady lines of visitors come for fresh local fish.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop emphasizes careful sourcing and handwork: Noto-area rice (a Koshihikari/Notohikari blend), local Noto soy sauce and vinegar, premium Ariake nori, and each piece prepared by hand.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is a lavish kaisen-don piled with 18 kinds of local and nearby seafood — including tuna and chu-toro, scallop, squid, sweet shrimp, sea urchin, salmon roe, crab and more — finished with gold leaf laid over the ikura. Premium nigiri sushi is the other draw.

anecdotes.text: The house kaisen-don is built from 18 types of fresh local and regional seafood over Noto-grown rice and finished with gold leaf, a presentation that has made it one of the market's most photographed bowls.
The kitchen closes for the day once the day's ingredients run out, so the shop can shut before its posted 16:00 closing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Omicho Market shop page, Tabelog and an onetabi feature confirm 60+ years of history, the signature 18-neta kaisen-don finished with gold leaf (placed on the ikura), rice from a Noto Koshihikari/Notohikari blend, local Noto soy sauce and vinegar, top-grade Ariake nori, and the practice of closing once the day's ingredients run out.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sushi and kaisen-don are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: An all-seafood sushi and raw-fish kitchen; raw fish and shellfish are handled throughout, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A famous, busy market sushi spot where lines are common; a little basic Japanese and patience help, and pointing at the picture menu for the kaisen-don works fine for a foreign student.

kz_kuroya.gf_detail: This is a Japanese izakaya built around soy sauce, miso, and bonito/seafood dashi, plus tempura and other fried items in shared oil. There is no gluten-free menu and no indication of celiac-safe handling. Not safe for celiac diners.
kz_kuroya.vegan_detail: The menu centers on local fish (nodoguro/throat perch, sashimi), Noto beef stew, and seafood; even vegetable dishes are typically prepared with fish dashi. There are no documented vegan options.
kz_kuroya.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat 18:00-23:00 (last order). Closed Wednesday and Sunday. Irregular closures possible. (One listing notes the kitchen runs to last order ~23:00; opening from 17:00 is also reported on Hot Pepper.)
kz_kuroya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kuroya is an owner-run izakaya near Kanazawa Station, opened by chef Ishiguro, who trained at いたる (Itaru) in Kakigibashi — one of Kanazawa's most famous and beloved izakaya. He brought that pedigree to his own small counter, where the cooking is built around top-quality local fis

chef_bio.background: Kuroya is an owner-run izakaya near Kanazawa Station, opened by chef Ishiguro, who trained at いたる (Itaru) in the Kakinokibatake district — one of Kanazawa's most famous and beloved izakaya. He brought that pedigree to his own small counter, where the cooking is built around top-quality local fish and Kaga vegetables.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on 'Kanazawa's deliciousness' — abundant, high-level dishes made from local fish and vegetables, paired with regional sake at an intimate counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Local Hokuriku seafood, including thick-cut, well-marbled iwashi (sardine) sashimi praised as melt-in-the-mouth, and assorted fresh sashimi platters served in wooden boxes; double-fried Gosashima sweet potato (slow-roasted, then fried to order) and other Kaga vegetable dishes; grilled fish such as buri (yellowtail) collar; and a daily-limited (about 20 servings) A4–A5 Noto-beef stew, tender enough to cut with chopsticks and served in a hot stone pot.

anecdotes.text: Chef Ishiguro honed his craft at the celebrated Kanazawa izakaya いたる (Itaru) before opening Kuroya near the station.
The signature beef stew is based on a recipe from the chef's parents, who run a Western-style restaurant (洋食店) in Toyama, and uses A4–A5 Noto beef; only about 20 servings are made each day.
The small counter regularly fills up right after opening, so reservations are strongly advised.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Food Japon and Tabelog confirm chef Ishiguro's training at Itaru, the location near Kanazawa Station, the fatty iwashi (sardine) sashimi described as melt-in-mouth, assorted wooden-box sashimi, the double-fried Gosashima sweet potato, Kaga vegetables, grilled yellowtail collar, and the ~20-serving-a-day A4–A5 Noto-beef stew from the chef's parents' Toyama yoshoku restaurant, plus the need for reservations. Neither source supports nodoguro sashimi or a roasted-nodoguro reservation dish, so those were removed.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen prepares tempura and other fried seafood/vegetable dishes, so shared frying oil and wheat batter make gluten cross-contact likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a traditional Kanazawa izakaya, dishes rely on regular (wheat-containing) soy sauce, miso, and seasonings; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is seafood- and meat-forward (nodoguro, sashimi, Noto-beef stew); vegetable dishes are typically finished with fish dashi, so no reliably vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, locally loved counter izakaya where some Japanese and a phone reservation (it fills up fast) will go a long way, so it suits a student comfortable ordering in basic Japanese.

Barley craft beer AND a barley stout (加賀棒茶スタウト) are on the official menu = gluten in a single shared kitchen. Rice-flour pancakes only by ingredient. — Prior: ⚠ Safety review 2026-07-02: downgraded dedicated→high. Fails 'dedicated': (a) no own-source whole-kitchen GF claim (グルテンフリー never appears; menu only says pancakes use rice flour); (b) gluten served on-premises (4 craft beers) + some sauces/toppings may contain gluten. Still above options: entire food menu in-house rice flour, widely celiac-recommended, strict celiacs report no reactions. — Prior note: Dedicated gluten-free pancake cafe. All pancakes are made from 100% Ishikawa-grown Koshihikari rice flour with no wheat — batter is rice flour plus meringue (whipped egg whites), milk, and a touch of salt. The whole menu is built around gluten-free rice flour, so this is a genuine destination for gluten-avoiders. Note: savory/lunch items (Noto pork roast, bacon eggs benedict, etc.) and toppings have not been individually allergen-verified, so a strict celiac should confirm specific sauces/sides directly; the cafe does not publish a formal cross-contamination protocol.
kz_cafe_tamon.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature rice flour pancakes contain egg whites (meringue) and milk, and most menu items use dairy (cream, butter, ice cream), eggs, or Noto pork. No vegan items are labeled. Gluten-free travelers are well served here, but vegans are not.

chef_bio.background: Cafe Tamon occupies a machiya townhouse more than 100 years old in a quiet corner of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district, just in front of Utasu Shrine and near the Hashiba-cho bus stop. The interior keeps the old house's exposed beams and nostalgic atmosphere, with table seating downstairs and traditional tatami seating upstairs.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe describes itself as 'people-friendly and earth-friendly,' built on three commitments: sustainable Ishikawa rice sourcing (including rice that would otherwise be discarded), local-production-for-local-consumption ingredient sourcing, and care for natural aromatics.
chef_bio.specialty: Pure rice flour pancakes made from 100% Ishikawa-grown Koshihikari rice flour, folded with meringue (whipped egg whites), milk, and a pinch of salt to create a famously fluffy, mochi-chewy texture. The gold-leaf pancake, dressed in Kanazawa's signature gold leaf, is a standout, alongside Goto Island sweet-potato Mont Blanc pancakes, Noto pork bacon eggs benedict pancakes, and savory Noto pork lunches.

anecdotes.text: The cafe draws on sacred water from a historic well ('Toshitsune's Sake Well') at the neighboring Utasu Shrine, cherished since the shrine's founding.
The gold-leaf rice flour pancake is especially popular with international visitors, pairing Kanazawa's status as Japan's leading gold-leaf producer with a wheat-free, 100% rice-flour batter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The cafe's own site and Kanazawa Biyori confirm the century-old Higashi-Chaya machiya in front of Utasu Shrine (with its Toshitsune Sake Well), downstairs table and upstairs tatami seating, the 100% Ishikawa Koshihikari rice-flour pancakes made with whipped egg-white meringue, milk and a little salt, the gold-leaf pancake popular with foreign visitors, and sweet-potato Mont Blanc and Noto-pork options; the exact founding year of the shrine's well is not stated, so the '1603' date was dropped.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The official site and menu publish no formal allergen or cross-contamination protocol; the cafe lists a direct phone line (076-255-0370) for dietary questions.

positives.text: All pancakes are made from 100% Ishikawa-grown Koshihikari rice flour with no wheat — the entire pancake concept is gluten-free, making this a genuine GF destination.
The batter contains only rice flour, meringue (egg whites), milk, and a little salt, so the core product avoids wheat thickeners entirely.

cultural_comfort.note: A foreign student will feel comfortable here — it is popular with international visitors (the gold-leaf pancake is a known draw) and the gluten-free concept is easy to understand, though staff communication is mostly in Japanese so a few polite words help.

gf_review.why: The venue makes ZERO gluten-free/allergen claim in its own Japanese text — 米粉 is celebrity-cafe (MEGUMI) / SDGs marketing, not a celiac protocol. Barley craft beer AND a barley stout (加賀棒茶スタウト) are on the official menu = gluten in a single shared kitchen. Rice-flour pancakes only by ingredient.

kz_morihachi_saryo_omicho.gf_detail: This is a traditional Japanese sweets (wagashi) tea salon. Core offerings — fresh seasonal sweets (上生菓子), yokan, dorayaki, anmitsu, kuzukiri, zenzai — are wheat-and-bean-based and made on a confectionery line that handles flour; matcha sweets are dusted and plated together with these. There is no dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen protocol documented, and cross-contact is essentially unavoidable. Not suitable for celiacs. A few items (plain matcha, some rakugan/agar-based sweets) may incidentally avoid wheat, but staff cannot guarantee this — ask only if you tolerate trace gluten.
kz_morihachi_saryo_omicho.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is advertised. Many traditional wagashi here are plant-based by nature (red-bean an, mochi, agar/kanten sweets, kuzukiri, tokoroten, and straight matcha or hojicha/sencha), but other sets include dairy, egg, or honey (cream, ice cream with kakigori, dorayaki, certain confections). Nothing is labeled, so a vegan would need to ask item-by-item; a matcha-with-an-based-wagashi or a kanten/anmitsu order is the most likely fit but not confirmed.
kz_morihachi_saryo_omicho.hours_raw: Tea salon: 09:30-17:00 daily (per official Tabelog info). Shop counter listed as 9:00-16:30 on the official site. Closed Jan 1-2 only.

chef_bio.background: Morihachi (森八) is one of Kanazawa's most storied confectioners, founded in 1625 and long honored as official sweet-maker (御用菓子司) to the Kaga Domain's Maeda lords. Its Omicho tea salon sits beside Omicho Market, the centuries-old covered market locals call 'Kanazawa's kitchen,' just a few minutes from Musashigatsuji. The salon is a calm, light-filled room with a small gallery and table seating that looks out onto the garden of the neighboring historic samurai residence.
chef_bio.philosophy: Roughly four centuries of traditional confectionery craft offered as a quiet pause in a busy market — premium tea and hand-made seasonal sweets enjoyed slowly, in view of a historic garden.
chef_bio.specialty: Matcha-and-seasonal-wagashi sets paired with the house's premium fresh sweets (上生菓子), alongside anmitsu, kuzukiri, zenzai, dorayaki, and Uji-matcha shaved ice (kakigori) in summer. The company's most famous confection is Choseiden (長生殿), a refined rakugan counted among Japan's three great wagashi.

anecdotes.text: Morihachi was founded in 1625 and served as the official confectioner to the Kaga Maeda domain; its signature Choseiden rakugan is regarded as one of Japan's three most famous wagashi.
The Omicho salon overlooks the garden of the adjacent historic samurai residence (Terashima Kuranin-tei) and pairs matcha with seasonal fresh sweets and summer Uji-matcha kakigori.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese Wikipedia confirms the 1625 (Kan'ei 2) founding, the Kaga-Maeda official-confectioner role and Choseiden's standing among Japan's three great wagashi; the morihachi.net menu confirms the Omicho salon's view over the Terashima Kuranin-tei samurai-residence garden, matcha with seasonal jonamagashi sets, summer Uji-matcha kakigori, and anmitsu/kuzukiri/zenzai/dorayaki.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wagashi-focused tea salon where flour-, wheat-, and bean-based sweets share preparation and plating; no gluten-free protocol is documented and cross-contact should be assumed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu mixes plant-based wagashi (an, mochi, kanten, kuzukiri) with dairy/egg items (kakigori toppings, dorayaki, certain confections); no vegan labeling, so cross-contact and hidden animal ingredients are possible.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: Plant-based side: 「ところてん」「豆かん」「くずきり」「あんみつ」「お抹茶・上生菓子セット」. Animal side: 「アイス 餡添（バニラ）」「アイス 餡添（抹茶）」「クリームあんみつ」 and 「どら焼き「宝達」」. The kakigori entries read 「かき氷　能登産ブルーベリー / かき氷　宇治抹茶 - 金沢氷室を使用した滑らかな口どけと森八特製の蜜でお召し上がり下さい」.

positives.text: Picture menu and clearly priced matcha-and-sweet sets make ordering straightforward; many traditional offerings (matcha, an-based and agar sweets) are incidentally plant-based.

kz_kureha.gf_detail: This is a traditional Japanese sweets cafe. The signature items are jo-namagashi (seasonal wagashi), matcha, kakigori, and parfaits. Wagashi and matcha sweets here are not gluten-free: dough, fillings, and accompaniments commonly involve wheat/wheat starch, and there are no documented gluten-free offerings or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_kureha.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is advertised. Some items (matcha with plain wagashi, kakigori with syrup) may be plant-based, but parfaits, cream zenzai, and hot sandwiches typically use dairy/egg. Anyone strictly vegan would need to ask about each item; nothing is documented as certified vegan.

chef_bio.background: Kureha occupies a preserved wooden-lattice machiya in Kanazawa's historic Higashi Chaya geisha district. It is run by Eritora, a Kaga Yuzen kimono house founded in 1776 (Anei 5, late Edo period) that specializes in the region's traditional hand-dyed silk. The shop pairs a Kaga Yuzen gallery and kimono-rental business with a small tea-cafe, so guests sip matcha surrounded by dyed textile artistry.
chef_bio.philosophy: Embodying the Kaga ethos of tradition, quiet luxury, and attention to detail; the ground-floor gallery displays dyed Kaga Yuzen works by a contemporary artist of the craft, so the kimono house's artistry surrounds the cafe table.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal jo-namagashi (upper-grade wagashi) served with matcha, plus Kaga bocha kakigori, parfaits, matcha cream zenzai, and matcha-filled hot sandwiches.

anecdotes.text: The ground floor holds the Kaga Yuzen gallery and shop with cafe seating in back, while the second floor's tatami zashiki rooms let you look out over the chaya street while you eat.
Beyond the cafe, Kureha offers Kaga Yuzen kimono rental, blending dining with a dress-up experience in the old quarter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site and a Kanazawa cafe blog confirm Kureha is the cafe arm of the Kaga Yuzen kimono house Eritora (founded 1776), a two-story machiya in Higashi Chaya with a ground-floor gallery/shop and upstairs tatami rooms overlooking the street, serving wagashi, matcha, kakigori, parfaits, zenzai and hot sandwiches, plus kimono rental.

cultural_comfort.note: A calm, traditional machiya tea-cafe where pointing at the matcha-and-wagashi menu works fine, but staff are unlikely to handle dietary restrictions in English, so come for the atmosphere rather than special requests.

kz_kikuichi.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a classic Kanazawa oden house whose dashi is built on Ohno soy sauce (made from wheat) and whose signature items are literally wheat gluten — kuruma-fu (車麩) and nama-fu (生麩). The simmering broth, soy sauce, and miso preparations all contain wheat. Not safe for celiac diners.
kz_kikuichi.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The oden broth is a bonito-and-kombu dashi (fish-based), and the menu centers on seafood and animal items such as crab face (kani-men) made from female snow crab, scallop/whelk (baigai), and white-miso dote-yaki. There are no documented vegan options; the shared simmering pot makes cross-contact with fish dashi unavoidable.
kz_kikuichi.hours_raw: 17:30-22:00 (closes earlier when ingredients run out), closed Tue and Wed
