chef_bio.background: A brick-fronted Western-style diner (yoshoku) founded in 1957 by Taduzou Otsuka. It is now run by the third generation, Masaki Otsuka, who took over from his father and second-generation owner Shoji Otsuka. The restaurant is widely regarded as the most famous home of Kanazawa's local specialty, Hunton Rice.
chef_bio.philosophy: Second-generation owner Shoji Otsuka held that 'diligently making delicious food matters most' (丁寧においしいものを作り続けることが大事), prioritizing quality and consistency over flash.
chef_bio.specialty: Hunton Rice — a plate of plain ketchup rice topped with silky, partly soft-set egg, fried marlin cutlets and fried shrimp, lavished with house tartar sauce and ketchup. The restaurant also has a devoted following for its beef-consomme-and-milk cream soup, pork steak on an iron plate, cream croquettes and omelette hayashi rice.

anecdotes.text: Hunton Rice was born here in the 1960s when the head chef under second-generation owner Shoji recreated a dish he remembered from his Tokyo apprenticeship; the name blends 'Han' (Hungarian) and 'ton' (French for tuna). The original choice to spread the egg over the rice rather than wrap it was unconventional at the time and drew attention.
Today roughly 70-80% of customers order the Hunton Rice, and long queues regularly form outside the shop.
A lesser-known house favorite is the velvety cream soup, built on a sauce veloute base with beef consomme and milk that turns subtly sweet as you eat.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ことりっぷとfood-japonで、1957年大塚太蔵造氏創業、二代目正治→三代目正樹、ハントンライスの由来（1960年代、東京修業時代の料理を再現／『ハン=ハンガリー』+『トン=仏語のマグロ』／卵を広げて乗せる形が話題）、来店客の7〜8割が注文・行列、正治氏の『丁寧においしいものを作り続けることが大事』を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes are breaded and deep-fried (marlin and shrimp fries, cream croquettes) in shared oil, with flour-based cream and white sauces throughout the menu — high gluten cross-contamination risk.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen works extensively with eggs, seafood, meat and dairy; the signature dish alone uses about three eggs per plate, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, no-reservation family-run diner where pointing at the famous Hunton Rice and a few basic Japanese greetings will carry you through; bring cash and be ready to queue.

kz_sashimiya.gf_detail: This is a seafood and Kaga-cuisine izakaya built around sashimi, seafood rice bowls, soy-sauce-based dishes, jibuni (which uses wheat-thickened sauce and soy), and tempura. Soy sauce, dashi, and wheat are pervasive, and no gluten-free menu or allergen handling is documented. Not safe for celiacs.
kz_sashimiya.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused restaurant whose entire identity is fresh fish, sashimi, seafood bowls, and Noto beef. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented, and dashi/fish stock underlies most cooked dishes. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kz_sashimiya.hours_raw: Weekdays (Mon-Fri): 10:30-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Saturdays, Sundays & holidays: 09:30-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Closed Jan 1-4.
kz_sashimiya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Sashimiya sits right inside Kanazawa's Omicho Market, the city's bustling fish market, and is run by a former fish merchant who turned decades of handling the day's catch into a kitchen. The connection to the surrounding stalls is direct: the seafood comes from fishmongers within

chef_bio.background: Sashimiya sits right inside Kanazawa's Omicho Market, the city's bustling fish market, and is run by a former fish merchant who turned decades of handling the day's catch into a kitchen. The connection to the surrounding stalls is direct: the seafood comes from fishmongers within the same market (Yamaka Suisan), so the sashimi reaches the plate while it is still firm and glossy.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner's stated aim is to draw out the natural umami of each ingredient through expert preparation rather than heavy seasoning, leaning on the freshness that comes from buying within the market.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen is known for generously piled seafood rice bowls (kaisen-don) heaped with tuna, crab, yellowtail, nodoguro/black-throat seaperch, salmon roe, and sea urchin — served over plain freshly-cooked Ishikawa Koshihikari rather than vinegared rice — alongside sashimi platters, nodoguro prepared several ways, tempura of Kaga vegetables, and the local Ishikawa specialty jibuni.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a former fishmonger who applies skills honed over many years in the fish trade to select and cut the day's catch.
Its signature seafood bowl is loaded with luxurious toppings like tuna, crab, yellowtail, nodoguro, salmon roe, and sea urchin, all sourced from fishmongers inside Omicho Market.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイトとcorezoで、元魚屋の店主が長年の技術で素材の旨みを引き出す、近江町市場内ヤマカ水産から仕入れ、まぐろ・蟹・ぶり・のど黒・いくら・うにの海鮮丼（酢飯でなく石川産コシヒカリの白飯）、刺身、治部煮、加賀野菜の天ぷらを確認。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Menu centers on sashimi, seafood bowls, tempura, and jibuni, all of which rely on soy sauce and dashi; tempura adds wheat batter. No gluten-free options are documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Entirely seafood- and meat-driven (sashimi, seafood bowls, Noto beef), with dashi-based cooked dishes; no vegan or vegetarian items are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, welcoming market izakaya used to tourists and accepting cards and QR payments, so a few words of Japanese and pointing at the seafood bowls will get you a great meal comfortably.

kz_cialda.gf_detail: This is a traditional Showa-era kissaten whose signature dishes are wheat-based: napolitan pasta, pizza toast, ham pilaf, and toast. There is no gluten-free menu and no indication of allergen accommodation. Not safe for celiacs.
kz_cialda.vegan_detail: A classic coffee shop serving meat- and dairy-based fare (ham pilaf, pizza toast, napolitan). Beverages include coffee and tea typically taken with milk. No documented vegan options.
kz_cialda.notes: [Mom & Pop] Cialda is a long-running retro coffee shop tucked away just steps from Omicho Market in central Kanazawa. Reported in 2024 to be 61 years old, it dates to roughly the early 1960s. Its sign is almost hidden behind a curtain of potted plants, giving it a hidden-away, easy-to-miss c

chef_bio.background: Cialda is a long-running retro coffee shop tucked away just steps from Omicho Market in central Kanazawa. Reported in 2024 to be 61 years old, it dates to roughly 1963. Its sign is almost hidden behind a curtain of potted plants, giving it a hidden-away, easy-to-miss charm even for locals who pass nearby.
chef_bio.specialty: Napolitan pasta is the standout dish (served with Tabasco and grated cheese on the side), alongside other kissaten classics like pizza toast — famously baked in the shop's old, temperature-uncontrollable 'magic' toaster — and pilaf, plus coffee and tea.

anecdotes.text: The deep interior blends Showa retro with Western vintage: arches and tiles, an amber-toned glow, brick walls in the back room with a striking double-arched wall, and an actual telephone booth standing inside (now dressed with flowers as a photo spot).

A blogger noted the shop is so screened by abundant potted plants that its signage is nearly invisible from a distance, and that the master, like many old kissaten owners, joked that the cups and saucers gradually stop matching in number over the years.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tacsp.net and kanazawa-drifter.net confirm the 61-year-old shop, Napolitan with Tabasco/cheese, the famous 'magic' toaster for pizza toast, arches/tiles/amber tone and the interior telephone booth; junkissa.blog.jp confirms plants hiding the sign, the brick double-arched back room, and the master's cups-and-saucers joke.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature menu is wheat-heavy (napolitan pasta, pizza toast, ham pilaf, toast); shared kitchen with no documented allergen handling.
gf_cross_contamination.source_wording: Tabelog carries no menu block for this shop. The wheat items survive only in the auto-generated 関連のキーワード cloud — ピラフ / ピザトースト / ナポリタン / ホットケーキ / カツカレー / チーズケーキ — and in a reviewer's title 「丁寧なピザトースト」 (大トロ（よっしー）, 2024/05 visit). Genre is 喫茶店. Nothing on the page mentions ham, allergens, or kitchen ha

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are built on ham, cheese, butter and dairy; no documented dairy-free or plant-based preparation.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: Dairy is evidenced by the keyword cloud only — チーズケーキ, ソフトクリーム, ウインナーコーヒー, メロンソーダ (i.e. cream-float), ガムシロップ. ハム and バター appear nowhere on the page.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, time-capsule local kissaten run in Showa style where little or no English is likely spoken and the menu is in Japanese, so a foreign student will be most comfortable with a guide or a translation app and a respectful, quiet approach. Note: smoking is permitted inside.

kz_pino.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The menu centers on wheat-based items — waffles, spaghetti, doria, curry roux and breaded/sauced Western dishes — and there is no celiac protocol or gluten-free labeling documented. Even the omurice is typically served in a wheat-flour-thickened sauce. Not suitable for strict celiacs.
kz_pino.vegan_detail: A classic yoshoku kissaten built around egg-heavy omurice, cream sauces (mentaiko cream, butter chicken curry, béchamel), parfaits and dairy-topped waffles. No vegan menu and no documented plant-based options; the core dishes rely on eggs, butter, cream and dairy.
kz_pino.hours_raw: 11:30-20:30 (L.O. 20:00). Closed Wednesdays per cafe sources; one listing also notes Tuesday closure, so confirm before a Tuesday visit. Popular with younger diners — 30+ minute waits are possible.
kz_pino.notes: [Mom & Pop] Pino is a Showa-era kissaten just a minute from the Katamachi 1-chome intersection in central Kanazawa, open for over 40 years with a look that has barely changed since it debuted — stained-glass windows, brick walls and red sofas all original to the space, which was once a UCC c

chef_bio.background: Pino is a Showa-era kissaten just a minute from the Katamachi 1-chome intersection in central Kanazawa (address Katamachi 2-7-6), open for over 40 years with a look that has barely changed since it debuted — stained-glass windows, brick walls and red sofas all original to the space, which was once a UCC coffee franchise location. It is run day to day by a husband-and-wife team.
chef_bio.philosophy: All sauces and dressings are made in-house, and coffee is brewed individually by siphon rather than batch-prepared, keeping the hand-made, unhurried character of a traditional kissaten.
chef_bio.specialty: Western-style comfort food anchored by a signature omurice served under double sauce (tomato and béchamel), with variations like mentaiko cream and butter-chicken-curry omurice, plus crispy waffles available in around 16-20 topping combinations and roughly 11 styles of parfait. The popular 'Yokubari Set' pairs a main with salad, a drink and a mini parfait or waffle.

anecdotes.text: The cafe draws multiple generations — some regulars first came as high schoolers and now bring their grandchildren — and on busy days the owner couple are said to walk roughly 10km inside the shop keeping up with the crowd.
Its enduring Showa-retro atmosphere has made it popular again with younger diners and tourists, with waits of 30 minutes or more possible at peak times.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kanazawa-tsu.com confirms the 40+ year run, the former UCC franchise, husband-wife operation, siphon coffee brewed to order, in-house sauces, double-sauce/mentaiko/butter-curry omurice, ~11 parfaits, ~20 waffle toppings, the 1,500-yen Yokubari Set, multi-generational regulars and the 10km figure; kawachibancan.com confirms the Showa retro look, red sofas, young clientele and 30-minute-plus waits.

positives.text: Sauces and dressings are all made in-house, so staff can describe what goes into a dish if you ask, though no formal allergen handling is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, busy old-school Showa-era kissaten where ordering is point-and-eat simple, but staff likely speak little English, so a few basic Japanese phrases or pointing at the picture menu will make the visit smooth.

kz_kappo_murai.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kaga-cuisine kappo built around tempura, soy-seasoned simmered dishes (jibuni), grilled fish and dashi-based cooking. Wheat (tempura batter, soy sauce) and dashi are central to the menu, and there is no documented gluten-free handling or dedicated equipment. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_kappo_murai.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused kappo specializing in nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), sashimi, crab, oysters and the soy/dashi-stewed Kaga dish jibuni. Dishes rely on fish, dashi and meat throughout, with no documented vegan menu or options.
kz_kappo_murai.hours_raw: 16:30-22:00 (dinner only per official site and Tabelog). One tourism listing also notes a 11:30-14:00 lunch service; dinner-only confirmed by official site.
kz_kappo_murai.notes: A long-established kappo on Korinbo's Seseragi-dori, an area renowned as one of Kanazawa's culinary streets and within easy reach of the historic samurai district. The restaurant has been serving for several decades (described as a 40- to 50-year establishment), spread over three

chef_bio.background: A long-established kappo on Korinbo's Seseragi-dori, an area renowned as one of Kanazawa's culinary streets and within easy reach of the historic Nagamachi samurai district. The restaurant reached its 50th anniversary, spread over three floors with a ground-floor counter and table seats, second-floor private tatami rooms and a large third-floor room that opens up for parties of up to two dozen.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen's stated approach values seasonality, carefully chosen local ingredients, and thoughtful presentation, putting heart and technique into each dish; the house motto is 'consideration for people, sincerity in cooking' (人に思いやり、料理に真心), under the theme of sending guests home with no regrets (後悔させません).
chef_bio.specialty: Kaga cuisine and seasonal seafood: salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), the soy-and-dashi simmered Kaga specialty jibuni, assorted sashimi, the house 'Murai special' sweet-shrimp (amaebi) tempura, seasonal natural Noto rock oysters, crab and pufferfish, and Kaga-vegetable tempura. Signature courses include Kaga kaiseki and a nodoguro course.

anecdotes.text: Located on Seseragi-dori, a celebrated dining street in central Kanazawa, the place is known as a discreet spot quietly favored by visiting celebrities.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official kappoumurai.jp confirms the 50th anniversary, three floors with ground-floor counter and upstairs tatami rooms (up to ~24 in the top room), the motto 人に思いやり・料理に真心, nodoguro, jibuni and amaebi tendon; kanazawa-kankoukyoukai.or.jp confirms the 後悔させません theme, salt-grilled nodoguro, sweet-shrimp/Kaga-vegetable tempura, crab and pufferfish; seseragi-st.com/hitosara.com note it is quietly favored by celebrities and serves Noto rock oysters.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu centers on tempura (wheat batter), soy-seasoned jibuni, and dashi-based dishes; no gluten-free handling is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kaga dishes such as jibuni and accompanying sauces use Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Cooking is built around fish, shellfish, meat and dashi; no vegan preparation or separation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional Japanese kappo where some Japanese language and familiarity with multi-course Kaga dining will help; reservations by phone and a basic grasp of the menu make for a smoother visit.

kz_nakatani_tofu.gf_detail: The shop's signature items are soy-based: soy milk soft serve and tofu ice cream, plus tofu, fried tofu (age) and okara. Tofu and soy milk are naturally wheat-free, so the core soy desserts are likely suitable for gluten-avoiders. However, this is a traditional neighborhood tofu shop with no documented allergen handling or celiac protocol, fried items (age) share frying, and cones/toppings are not confirmed gluten-free. A celiac should ask and stick to the plain soy soft serve or tofu rather than fried products.
kz_nakatani_tofu.vegan_detail: A handmade tofu shop whose draw for plant-based eaters is its 豆乳ソフトクリーム (soy milk soft serve) and とうふアイスクリーム (tofu ice cream), both made from soybeans rather than dairy, along with fresh tofu, fried tofu (age) and okara to take away. The soft serve and tofu products are plant-based by nature, though the shop is a tofu maker, not a self-declared vegan business, so individual recipes (e.g. any added ingredients in flavored items) are not certified. The soy milk soft serve is seasonal, typically sold April through October.
kz_nakatani_tofu.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 10:00-19:00 / Sun soy-milk soft serve only
kz_nakatani_tofu.notes: A small, long-established handmade tofu shop tucked into the historic Nishi Chaya geisha district near Nomachi. It keeps the unassuming feel of an old neighborhood tofu maker, selling fresh tofu, fried tofu (age), okara and other soy goods, with an elderly proprietor who minds th

roles: 手造り豆腐店（handmade tofu shop）
chef_bio.background: A small handmade tofu shop, founded roughly 40 years ago as a wholesale tofu maker, tucked into the historic Nishi Chaya geisha district near Nomachi. It keeps the unassuming feel of an old neighborhood tofu maker, selling fresh tofu, fried tofu (age), okara and other soy goods, with an elderly proprietor who minds the shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Carefully selected soybeans and good water turned into honest, traditional tofu — the soy desserts let visitors taste that tofu character in a cone.
chef_bio.specialty: 豆乳ソフトクリーム (soy-milk soft serve, ~350 yen), a rich, lightly sweetened cone made with two-to-three times the usual soybeans, sold only in the warmer months (about April-October); and とうふアイスクリーム (tofu ice cream, ~350 yen, year-round), a light gelato-style dessert made by working the shop's own silk tofu into the base. Locals note both go well with a drizzle of local Ohno soy sauce. Alongside the desserts the shop sells handmade tofu, age and okara.

anecdotes.text: Visitors describe the soy milk soft serve as having a concentrated soybean flavor with restrained sweetness and a smooth, almost tofu-like texture rather than ordinary dairy ice cream.

One reviewer noted the elderly proprietor sits outside and comes into the shop when customers ring a bell, underlining how intimate and family-run the shop is, and that the soft serve is only sold in the warmer months.
The shop's tofu ice cream, made from its own handmade silk tofu, is described as light in flavor and said to pair well with a touch of the region's Ohno soy sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 4travel.jp confirms the soy-milk soft serve's concentrated flavor and restrained sweetness, the smooth tofu-like texture, the elderly proprietor and bell, and warm-season-only sales; co-trip.jp confirms the shop is ~40 years old (started wholesale), the soft serve uses 2-3x the soybeans and sells Apr-Oct, the year-round tofu ice cream is made from the shop's silk tofu, and both pair with local Ohno soy sauce.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tofu ice cream is sometimes eaten with a touch of soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so gluten-avoiders should skip the soy sauce option.

positives.text: The signature items — soy milk soft serve and tofu ice cream — are made from soybeans rather than dairy, making the core offerings plant-based.
positives.why: 'Rather than dairy' is the record's inference, not anything a source states - soft-serve mixes routinely carry milk solids, so this is an unearned assurance to a vegan. What IS documented and should be cited instead: the plain tofu is 「北陸のエンレイ大豆と能登の塩田にがりだけを使った豆腐」 (soybeans and nigari only) at co-tri

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny old neighborhood tofu shop run by an elderly proprietor with essentially no English, so point at the soft serve, have cash ready, and a few words of Japanese will help.

kz_rakugan_moroeya_nishicha.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. Rakugan is traditionally pressed rice-flour/wasanbon sugar candy and is often wheat-free, and zenzai (red bean soup) is rice-and-bean based, but namagashi (上生菓子) and seasonal items can contain wheat, and no allergen information or cross-contact controls are published. Celiac diners must ask about each specific item.
kz_rakugan_moroeya_nishicha.vegan_detail: Traditional Kaga wagashi here (rakugan, zenzai, namagashi) are typically plant-based, made from rice, sugar (wasanbon/wasanbon-tou), and adzuki beans without dairy or egg, so vegan-suitable options likely exist. However, the shop publishes no vegan labeling and kakigori syrups/toppings and some namagashi may vary, so confirm ingredients per item before ordering.
kz_rakugan_moroeya_nishicha.hours_raw: 10:00-17:00 (L.O. 16:30); closed Tuesdays (open on public holidays, with Wednesday taken as substitute closure)
kz_rakugan_moroeya_nishicha.notes: [Mom & Pop] Rakugan Moroeya is a Kanazawa wagashi house founded in 1849 (late Edo period), describing itself as having walked the same path as the city for over 170 years. chef_bio.background: Rakugan Moroeya is a Kanazawa wagashi house founded in 1849 (Kaei 2, late Edo period), describing itself as having walked the same path as the city for over 170 years. In 2012 it opened the Nishichaya Karyo cafe, named Ajiwai, in the historic Nishi Chaya geisha district of Nomachi, combining a retail shop with a bright, welcoming tea space where travelers can shop and rest.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house aims to honor the tradition of Kaga meika (famous Kaga sweets) and traditional manufacturing methods while continuing to refine flavors and products beloved in contemporary times.
chef_bio.specialty: Rakugan (pressed wasanbon-sugar candy) is the house specialty, alongside seasonal Japanese sweets, zenzai (sweet red-bean soup), kakigori (shaved ice) in the warmer months, and jonamagashi (premium fresh sweets). Signature confections include Hojo-gashi (方丈菓子), Kaga Hosho (加賀宝生), and Hana-usagi (花うさぎ).

anecdotes.text: Founded in 1849 near the end of the Edo period, Moroeya says it has shared Kanazawa's path for more than 170 years.
The Nishichaya Karyo cafe opened in 2012 as a combined shop and tea house in the Nishi Chaya district, designed as a bright place to shop and take a break while traveling.

positives.text: Traditional menu of rakugan, zenzai, kakigori and namagashi is largely rice-, bean- and sugar-based, which often suits plant-based diners, though no allergen labeling is published.

kz_jiba_ryori_to_shuko_kise.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature Kaga jibuni is made with wheat-flour-coated meat and Kanazawa fu (sudare-fu / nama-fu, which are wheat gluten), and the kaiseki menu relies on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi throughout. No gluten-free or allergy accommodations are mentioned anywhere. Celiac travelers should treat this as unsafe.
kz_jiba_ryori_to_shuko_kise.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian-friendly. This is a seasonal Kaga kaiseki house centered on fish, eel, duck/chicken/pork, and seafood, with dashi-based broths throughout. No vegan or vegetarian menu is offered.
kz_jiba_ryori_to_shuko_kise.hours_raw: Official site: Lunch 11:00-15:00 (last seating 13:00, reservation-only, larger groups), Dinner 18:00-22:00. Tabelog: 12:00-14:00 and 18:00-23:00 (L.O. 21:30). Reservation-only operation. Irregular days off.
kz_jiba_ryori_to_shuko_kise.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kanazawa Saiya is an owner-run seasonal kaiseki restaurant a short walk from the east side of Kanazawa Station, working with fresh local fish, Kaga vegetables, and seasonal ingredients sourced from around Japan, paired with local sake.

chef_bio.background: Kanazawa Saiya is an owner-run seasonal kaiseki restaurant a short walk from the east side of Kanazawa Station, working with fresh local fish, Kaga vegetables, and seasonal ingredients sourced from around Japan, paired with local sake from Ishikawa, Toyama and Fukui.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner emphasizes uncompromising, meticulous preparation paired with seasonal ingredients to create hospitality (妥協のない仕込みと旬の食材が織り成すおもてなし).
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is Kaga jibuni served as a small individual hot pot (加賀治部煮小鍋仕立て). While the classic Kanazawa dish uses wheat-flour-coated duck or chicken with fu (wheat gluten) and root vegetables, this house makes its version with slow-braised pork belly (豚三枚肉) alongside Kaga nama-fu and root vegetables. Other seasonal dishes include white-soy-glazed eel, flounder-and-squash layered tempura, and seasonal rice cooked in clay pots.

anecdotes.text: The kaiseki is offered at the more approachable prices typical of an individually owned restaurant, drawing both Kanazawa locals and visitors who return as regulars.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kanazawasaiya.com confirms the owner-run seasonal kaiseki near Kanazawa Station, local Kaga vegetables and fish, the 妥協のない仕込み motto, curated Hokuriku sake, and the signature 加賀治部煮小鍋仕立て made with pork belly (豚三枚肉), root vegetables and local nama-fu; the menu page confirms the white-soy-glazed eel and flounder-and-squash layered tempura and clay-pot seasonal rice. Owner name is not published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature jibuni uses wheat-flour-coated meat and Kanazawa fu (sudare-fu and nama-fu, which are wheat gluten), so wheat is central to the kitchen and shared prep is likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Seasoning is built on traditional Japanese soy sauce and dashi (including a white-soy eel glaze), which contain wheat; no wheat-free soy alternative is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are dashi-, fish-, and meat-based throughout, so even vegetable items are not prepared vegan.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a reservation-only owner-run kaiseki house where some Japanese ability or a Japanese-speaking helper to book and communicate dietary needs will make the visit much smoother for a foreign student.

kz_sobadokoro_way.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The house soba is nihachi (二八), made with 20% wheat flour blended into the buckwheat, and is served with wheat-based soba dashi/tsuyu. There is no gluten-free option and no indication of celiac accommodation. Not safe for those with celiac disease or wheat allergy.
kz_sobadokoro_way.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The fixed "osoba-zen" set is built around fish-dashi-based soba broth and seasonal small dishes; the owner is a fisherman who serves his own-caught sashimi when available, and add-on options include herring (nishin) and nameko soba. No documented vegan set.
kz_sobadokoro_way.hours_raw: Sun & Mon 11:00-14:00 (open Sun and Mon only; check Instagram for latest info)
kz_sobadokoro_way.notes: [Mom & Pop] Sobadokoro WAY opened in autumn 2024 on the corner of the Teramachi 1-chome intersection, inside a renovated building that previously housed a hair salon and a remake shop. The interior was designed by the local architecture and design studio SWAY DESIGN, giving the small space a

chef_bio.background: Sobadokoro WAY opened in autumn 2024 on the corner of the Teramachi 1-chome intersection, inside a renovated building that previously housed a hair salon and a remake shop. The interior was designed by the local architecture and design studio SWAY DESIGN, giving the small space a modern, stylish feel complete with a vacuum-tube amplifier audio system.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner wants guests to eat things freshly made with real care and time ('手間ひまかけた出来たてを食べて欲しい').
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the 'osoba-zen' (おそば膳), a 1,500 yen set built around freshly hand-cut nihachi soba made from Nagano-grown buckwheat flour, served with a seasonal small dish and rice. The soba can be swapped for grated-radish oroshi soba, warm nameko soba, or nishin (herring) soba for an extra 300 yen.

anecdotes.text: Owner Fujita is a soba craftsman with more than 50 years of experience, hand-cutting each batch of nihachi soba himself.
He also runs a soba-and-sweets shop in Komatsu and is a fisherman who serves his own freshly caught sashimi when the previous day's catch allows.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: weekend-kanazawa.com confirms the autumn-2024 opening on Teramachi 1-chome in a former beauty salon/remake shop, the SWAY DESIGN interior, the 1,500-yen おそば膳 of hand-cut nihachi soba from Nagano flour with a seasonal side and rice, the +300-yen oroshi/nameko/nishin swaps, owner Fujita's 50+ years, his Komatsu main shop, the fisherman-sashimi story, and the 手間ひまかけた出来たて motto.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House soba is nihachi (二八), made with 20% wheat flour, so the noodles themselves contain gluten and there is no gluten-free option.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soba is served with a traditional dashi/tsuyu, which in soba shops is wheat-soy-sauce based; no gluten-free tsuyu is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The set centers on fish-dashi broth and seafood (sashimi, herring), so vegan separation is not offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 7-seat counter run by a veteran soba craftsman with limited Sunday/Monday-only hours, so a little Japanese and patience help; come ready to order the set course and enjoy the quiet, music-filled space.

kz_kissa_nobar.gf_detail: A retro coffee shop whose signature items are hotcakes, pudding parfaits and Napolitan-style dishes — all wheat-based or served with wheat sides. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented, and this is not a celiac-safe venue.
kz_kissa_nobar.vegan_detail: The menu centers on dairy-and-egg desserts (homemade pudding, parfaits with whipped cream, hotcakes) and coffee. No vegan options are documented.
kz_kissa_nobar.notes: [Mom & Pop] A nostalgic Showa-era pure coffee house that has been welcoming locals for more than 40 years. chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa, near the Arimatsu intersection just south of the Nishi Chaya geisha district
chef_bio.background: A nostalgic Showa-era pure coffee house that has been welcoming locals for more than 40 years. The cafe is run as a husband-and-wife operation: the master handcrafts the desserts one by one while his wife decorates the plates with carefully cut fruit and whipped cream. The interior has barely changed since it opened, with a stained-glass wall, a chandelier, wine-red sofas, brickwork and framed paintings preserving a gorgeous, slightly bubble-era Western look.
chef_bio.philosophy: Seating and sight lines are arranged so guests never feel watched by other customers, making it an unusually relaxing place to linger over coffee.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is the homemade pudding (自家製プリン, around 500 yen), a firm, not-too-sweet custard topped with decoratively cut fruit and cream; it also appears as a pudding parfait. Other beloved items include Ogura hotcakes (小倉ホットケーキ) and coffee.

anecdotes.text: The cafe is locally famous because actress Yoh Yoshida (吉田羊) worked here as a part-time staff member before her acting career.

Soft light filtering through the stained glass makes the menus and desserts a popular photo subject, and the master-and-mama team handcraft each pudding with restrained sweetness so it pairs well with coffee or tea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: weekend-kanazawa.com confirms the 40+ year run near the Arimatsu intersection, the husband-wife operation (master makes the desserts, wife decorates them), the brick/stained-glass/privacy-arranged interior, the 500-yen 自家製プリン handmade one by one, and the Yoh Yoshida (吉田羊) part-time backstory; apple2019a.hatenablog.com corroborates the stained-glass light and the restrained-sweetness pudding.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional Showa-era kissaten run by an older couple with no English menu and cash-only payment, so a foreign student would be most comfortable bringing a Japanese-speaking friend or a translation app.

kz_sushi_kibatani.gf_detail: This is a traditional Edomae sushi counter and is not safe for celiacs. Sushi is built on vinegared rice and seafood brushed with nikiri/tsume sauces and served with soy sauce, all of which are wheat-based. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented. Travelers with celiac disease should not rely on this restaurant.
kz_sushi_kibatani.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused omakase sushi restaurant centered entirely on fish sourced daily from Himi and Shinminato ports (yellowtail, abalone, uni, kohada, crab). There is no vegan or vegetarian menu and the entire concept is animal-based. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kz_sushi_kibatani.hours_raw: 17:00-21:00 (seatings reported around 17:00 and 20:30); closed Sundays plus irregular holidays. Completely reservation-based.
kz_sushi_kibatani.notes: After starting out as a salaryman, Kibatani found his calling working at a fish shop in Tokyo's Tsukiji market, which sparked a passion for seafood. He trained in Edomae technique at respected sushi houses including Yoshiura in Funabashi and the celebrated Sushi Aoki in Ginza, th

chef_bio.origin: Born 1973 in Toyama Prefecture; his family runs a fresh-fish business in Oyabe (Ishidō), giving him fish-sourcing in his blood.
chef_bio.background: After starting out as a salaryman, Kibatani found his calling working at a fish shop in Tokyo's Tsukiji market, which sparked a passion for seafood. He trained in Edomae technique at respected sushi houses including Yoshiura in Funabashi and the celebrated Sushi Aoki in Ginza, then spent years as a traveling (catering) sushi chef before opening his own counter, Sushi Kibatani, in Kanazawa's Hikosan-cho district in 2016. The 9-seat counter has since earned a Michelin one-star and become one of Kanazawa's hardest tables to book.
chef_bio.philosophy: Kibatani speaks with gratitude about his hard years as a traveling chef and treats running his own place as a privilege, devoting himself to letting guests experience the full richness of the Hokuriku sea. He keeps learning even after success - in summer 2022 he closed for about three months (June-August) to apprentice in uni handling in Hokkaido.
chef_bio.specialty: Edomae sushi built on premium Hokuriku fish landed daily at Himi and Shinminato ports (and Nanao/Uozu) - yellowtail, abalone, horse mackerel, uni and crab. His signature is kohada, cured with meticulous Edomae technique adjusted to the weather and each individual fish. Dashi is shaved fresh from katsuobushi at the counter, and he uses binchotan charcoal for precise grilling; one memorable course pairs hairy crab with a rich, almost French-style uni sauce over rice.

anecdotes.text: Despite running one of Kanazawa's most sought-after sushi counters, Kibatani took a roughly three-month hiatus in summer 2022 to train in uni preparation in Hokkaido.
A signature course pairs hairy crab with a rich uni sauce over rice, described as enveloping the crab's delicate sweetness in a French-style richness.
His signature kohada is cured with Edomae technique that he adjusts to the day's weather and the character of each fish.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hitosara.com confirms b.1973 Toyama, the Tsukiji awakening, training at Yoshiura (Funabashi) and 鮨青木 (Ginza), the traveling-chef years, the 2016 Hikosan-cho opening and the weather/fish-adjusted kohada; food-japon.com confirms the family fishmonger in Oyabe (小矢部石動), sourcing at Himi/Shinminato/Nanao/Uozu, counter-shaved katsuobushi dashi, binchotan, the hairy-crab-and-uni-sauce dish and the June-August 2022 Hokkaido uni training; kanazawa.xyz confirms the Michelin one-star and 9-seat counter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Edomae sushi is built on vinegared rice, soy-based nikiri/tsume sauces, and soy sauce, so gluten is pervasive throughout the meal; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) and brushed nikiri/tsume sauces are integral to the sushi served here.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire omakase is seafood-based with fish-derived dashi (freshly shaved katsuobushi at the counter); there are no vegan dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a high-end, completely reservation-only omakase sushi counter where the chef serves you directly, so a foreign student should expect a formal Japanese-only dining experience and a substantial budget (roughly 20,000 yen and up).

Scones are the documented exception (not gluten-free), so confirm per item. Not a certified celiac-dedicated kitchen, but rice-flour baking is the core focus, so confidence is high for the muffins/pound cakes/florentines.
kz_natural_grocery_store_mi.vegan_detail: The cafe's handmade baked goods (muffins, scones, pound cakes, florentines) and drinks are entirely plant-based, made without eggs, butter or dairy. The attached shop also stocks vegan-certified products. Sweets and house-made items are fully vegan.
kz_natural_grocery_store_mi.hours_raw: 10:00-17:00. Closed Tue and irregular days off.
kz_natural_grocery_store_mi.notes: midoriya is run by Takahashi Tomoko, a former high-school teacher who, after becoming a mother, reconsidered the importance of what we eat and decided to open a natural-foods shop. It first opened in November 2020 on the second floor of her family's longstanding boutique. When th

chef_bio.background: midoriya is run by Takahashi Tomoko, who came to natural food not from the kitchen but from an earlier career in interior design (she holds a second-class architect's license) and apparel/customer service. While on maternity leave with her third child she was struck by how hard it was to find genuinely additive-free foods, and resolved to open a shop selling things she had chosen herself. It first opened in November 2020 on the second floor of her family's longstanding boutique. When the boutique closed she moved the shop down to the ground floor and reopened in May 2023 with a larger sales floor and a new cafe space.
chef_bio.philosophy: She personally curates every product from a parent's point of view, choosing additive-free, organic and vegan-certified items that are genuinely good for body, mind and the environment. The cafe extends that ethic with reusable-tumbler discounts and sustainable sourcing.
chef_bio.specialty: House-made vegan baked goods, many made with rice flour instead of wheat — muffins and pound cakes among them — plus herbal teas, Japanese black tea, craft cola and coffee. Note that not every item is gluten-free (the scones, for example, are made with wheat), so anyone avoiding gluten should ask about each product rather than assume.

anecdotes.text: The shop occupies the family's former boutique building on Kanazawa's Omotesando shopping street, described as over 90 years old; the renovation kept antique furniture and vintage-fabric upholstery from the boutique era, giving the eat-in space a retro charm.
A signature item is a rice-flour muffin made with pesticide-free organic lemon and a vegan custard, served alongside natural herbal tea.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kigyokomachi.com (via search) confirms the owner is Takahashi Tomoko, whose background was interior design (2nd-class architect) and apparel, and who moved into natural food on maternity leave with her third child; weekend-kanazawa.com confirms the Nov 13 2020 second-floor opening and May 2023 ground-floor cafe reopening, the organic/vegan-certified curation and the organic-lemon/vegan-custard rice-flour muffin; manpuku-kanazawa.com confirms the vegan baked goods are mostly rice-flour/gluten-free EXCEPT the scones (wheat) and the kept antique furniture/vintage-fabric seating; bonno-web.com confirms the boutique building is over 90 years old (築90余年) on Kanazawa's Omotesando.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Baked goods are made fresh in an open kitchen; most are rice-flour gluten-free, but scones are not gluten-free, so wheat is present in the same kitchen. No celiac-grade cross-contamination protocol is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All house-made baked goods and drinks are stated to contain no animal-derived ingredients (no eggs, butter or dairy), so vegan cross-contact risk in the cafe items is low.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner curates products with a focus on items children can safely enjoy and labels baked goods as egg/butter/wheat-free where applicable, but no formal allergy protocol is documented; ask about specific items in person.
staff_allergy_handling.why: Curation-for-children and the absence of any documented protocol are both on the page; the in-store allergen-labelling assertion is not evidenced anywhere I could reach. Drop that clause - it is the kind of detail a celiac would act on.

positives.text: Sweets are made with rice flour and are vegan, with gluten-free options clearly the focus of the menu.
Egg-free and dairy-free options are available, with explicit vegan and gluten-free framing throughout the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A warm, small solo-run natural-foods cafe where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the rice-flour sweets will get you a friendly welcome; English service is not guaranteed.

gf_review.why: BOTH a grocery (sealed GF goods, low CC) AND a café with an OPEN kitchen that bakes WHEAT scones alongside rice-flour items, zero documented cross-contact controls; sources even contradict on whether scones are wheat. Sealed goods are fine, prepared café food is not celiac-safe.

kz_kazuemachi_oryori_ichiri.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering documented. This is a traditional Japanese seasonal/kaiseki house built around dashi and soy sauce, with courses centered on seafood and Kaga vegetables. Soy sauce (typically wheat-based) and wheat-containing seasonings are integral to the cooking, so it is not celiac-safe. No dedicated fryer or allergen protocol is published; a celiac traveler would need to inquire directly in advance.
kz_kazuemachi_oryori_ichiri.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. The kitchen is "particular about fish" and courses are built on seasonal seafood plus fish/kombu dashi, so standard courses are not vegan or vegetarian. The restaurant features Kaga vegetables and local sake, so a plant-forward request might be accommodated for a reserved course, but this is not confirmed and must be arranged with the restaurant ahead of time.
