chef_bio.background: Ichirin occupies a renovated Kanazawa machiya on the Asano River in the historic Kazuemachi tea district, a townhouse that was the later-life residence of the American printmaker Clifton Karhu. The interior still displays pieces from his collection, so diners eat surrounded by his artwork while taking in the Edo-period atmosphere of the riverside teahouse quarter.
chef_bio.philosophy: An emphasis on Kanazawa's seasonal local ingredients and regional sake, served in a setting that preserves the heritage of a Kazuemachi townhouse.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal multi-course Japanese cuisine built on local seafood and Kaga vegetables, paired with local Ishikawa sake; the kitchen is noted for being particular about its fish. Lunch sets such as the Hanakago box make the cuisine approachable at midday.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant is set in the former home of American woodblock printmaker Clifton Karhu, who spent his final years in this Kazuemachi townhouse; his art is shown throughout the dining space, including a distinctive blue-plaster-walled Japanese room.
It is the riverside Kanazawa restaurant operated by the local MOMIJI GROUP, which also runs other Japanese and Western dining venues in the city, opened in this Kazuemachi location.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ichi-rin.com confirms the renovated Kazuemachi machiya on the Asano River, that it was Clifton Karhu's final residence with his artwork displayed (including a blue-plaster Japanese room), the seasonal local cuisine with Kaga vegetables and local sake, and the attention to fish; momiji-group.com confirms it is a MOMIJI GROUP venue.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional Japanese kaiseki-style kitchen relying on soy sauce and dashi-based seasonings; no gluten-free protocol or dedicated equipment is documented, so cross-contamination with wheat should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Cuisine is built around standard Japanese seasonings including soy sauce, which is typically brewed with wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Courses center on seafood and almost certainly use fish/kombu dashi; no separate vegan preparation line is documented, so animal-derived stocks should be assumed throughout.

positives.text: Reservations are required and arranged by phone or an online form, giving diners a clear channel to communicate dietary restrictions in advance.

cultural_comfort.note: A polished course-style Japanese restaurant where a reservation and a few words of Japanese (or a translation app) go a long way; staff are used to guests but the experience is formal, so book ahead and flag any dietary needs when you reserve.

kz_kappo_uotsune.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a Kaga kappo built around dashi, soy sauce and seasonal fish. The signature jibuni is served with sudare-fu (wheat gluten) and a soy-and-mirin broth, and dishes use wheat-based soy sauce throughout. No dedicated gluten-free preparation. The kitchen does say it accepts allergy/dietary inquiries by direct phone, so a celiac diner would need to call ahead and discuss in detail — but it should not be considered celiac-safe.
kz_kappo_uotsune.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is centered on fish (nodoguro, sashimi) and duck (jibuni), and nearly everything is built on bonito/fish dashi. Vegetables are seasonal but prepared with animal-based broths and soy seasonings. The kitchen accepts allergy/dietary inquiries by phone, but there is no documented vegan offering.
kz_kappo_uotsune.hours_raw: 17:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:30); some listings give 17:00-23:00 (L.O. 22:00). Closed Sundays and holidays (open for groups of 10+ by reservation).
kz_kappo_uotsune.notes: [Mom & Pop] Uotsune is a family-run kappo set in a Taisho-era building on the embankment of the Asano River, just across from the Higashi Chaya District and near the Ume-no-hashi and Asanogawa-ohashi bridges. The weathered old structure is part of the draw: second-floor tatami rooms look out

chef_bio.background: Uotsune is a family-run kappo set in a building that keeps its Taisho-era character, on the embankment of the Asano River in Namikimachi, just across from the Kazuemachi and Higashi Chaya districts and near the Asanogawa-ohashi bridge. The weathered old structure is part of the draw: second-floor tatami rooms look out over the river, framing cherry blossoms in spring and colored leaves in autumn.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house runs on a simple motto — 'oishikute yasui' (美味しく安く), delicious and affordable — pairing seasonal Kaga ingredients with the changing views of the Asano River.
chef_bio.specialty: Kaga local cuisine led by duck jibuni — duck simmered with sudare-fu wheat gluten and seasonal vegetables in a soy-and-mirin broth — alongside salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), sashimi, and seasonal fish and vegetables.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant sits in a building that has kept its Taisho-era character, with upstairs river-view rooms that change with the four seasons of the Asano River.
The kitchen states it does not use automated reservation systems and prefers direct contact, and welcomes inquiries about allergies and dietary needs.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: uotsune01.sakura.ne.jp confirms the Namikimachi/Asano-River location, second-floor river-view rooms, the 美味しく安く motto, salt-grilled nodoguro and duck dishes, and the no-automated-reservation, allergy-welcoming policy; kanazawa-kankoukyoukai.or.jp and a Tabelog/search listing confirm the Asanogawa-ohashi setting across from Kazuemachi/Higashi Chaya and, notably, that the building retains its Taisho-era appearance (大正時代の佇まいを残す). The 'handed down from the previous owner' framing of the motto could not be verified and was softened.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature jibuni is made with sudare-fu (wheat gluten) and a soy-sauce-based broth, and the kitchen relies on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi across the menu; not celiac-safe.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kaga kappo cooking here uses standard wheat-based soy sauce in jibuni and seasonings throughout.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are built on fish/bonito dashi and feature duck and seafood; vegetable items are not prepared vegan.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The official site states the restaurant accepts inquiries about allergies and dietary restrictions and prefers direct phone contact over automated systems.

positives.text: Kitchen is open to allergy/dietary questions when contacted directly by phone before the visit.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional family-run riverside kappo where some Japanese helps; reservations are taken by phone and the kitchen prefers direct contact, so calling ahead (ideally in Japanese) and being ready to discuss dishes makes for a smoother visit.

kz_sobadokoro_anan.gf_detail: This is a hand-made soba shop. The noodles are made with Hokkaido buckwheat flour but, as with virtually all Japanese soba, are not certified gluten-free and almost always contain wheat flour binder; broths and dipping sauces are soy-sauce based (wheat-containing). Not suitable for celiacs. No gluten-free accommodation is documented.
kz_sobadokoro_anan.vegan_detail: Menu centers on duck (Zao duck seiro), egg yolk, Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, and seafood/vegetable tempura, with dashi- and soy-sauce-based broths. No vegan offerings are documented.
kz_sobadokoro_anan.notes: [Mom & Pop] A casual hand-made soba house run by a welcoming female proprietor. The noodles are hand-cut daily using buckwheat flour from the Isoya region of Hokkaido, prized for its aroma and smooth, easy-to-eat texture, and the kitchen leans on local Ishikawa vegetables and seasonal ingred

chef_bio.origin: Opened March 1, 2022 in Kanazawa's Musashi-machi (Residence Musashi 1F), a short walk from Omicho Market, on the site of a former soba shop (元たんば屋 Tanbaya).
chef_bio.background: A casual hand-made soba house run by a welcoming female proprietor. The noodles are hand-cut daily using buckwheat flour from the Isoya region of Hokkaido, prized for its aroma and smooth, easy-to-eat texture, and the kitchen leans on local Ishikawa vegetables and seasonal ingredients.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner wants guests to enjoy the meal all the way through without tiring of it (最後まで飽きずに楽しんでほしい), which shapes the varied, lightly inventive menu; the duck seiro is even built to shift in flavor with yuzu and shiso as you eat.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is tsuke-kamo seiro (duck seiro, ~1,800 yen): freshly hand-cut soba dipped in a warm, mellow broth built on Zao duck. Other standouts include a playful 'cheese soba' with Parmigiano-Reggiano and egg yolk (~1,300 yen) and bukkake oroshi soba with grated daikon (~1,000 yen).

anecdotes.text: The shop sits on the former site of the soba restaurant Tanbaya, set back from the main street in the Musashi area near Omicho Market.
Run solo by a kind female owner, the casual counter is described as especially comfortable for women dining alone.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 週末金沢・tacsp・かなざわ速報で、2022年3月1日開業、元たんば屋跡、北海道・雨竜(磯谷)産そば粉、蔵王産の鴨だしの鴨せいろ(1,800円)、女性店主による一人営業、『最後まで飽きずに』という思いを確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Hand-made soba is made and cut in a flour-heavy kitchen; wheat-based binder and shared surfaces make cross-contamination effectively certain.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dipping broths and sauces are soy-sauce based, which standardly contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Kitchen handles duck, egg, cheese, and seafood/vegetable tempura; no vegan-segregated preparation is documented.
vegan_cross_contact.why: Strike “seafood/vegetable tempura” — no source places a fryer in this kitchen, and it reads like it drifted in from a neighbouring listing. Duck, egg and Parmigiano stand on their own and are enough to justify the vegan “no”. Also refresh the hours: Tabelog now gives 水・木・金・土 11:30-15:00 / 17:00-21:0

cultural_comfort.note: A warm, solo-female-owner counter shop where dining alone is easy and welcome; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will go a long way, as English is unlikely.

kz_buemon.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Soba noodles here are made with sarashina (refined buckwheat) flour blended with wheat and roasted-tea powder, and soba is typically served with a wheat-based soy-sauce dashi tsuyu. No gluten-free menu or precautions are documented. Not safe for celiacs.
kz_buemon.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is documented. Soba is traditionally served with a katsuo/dashi-based dipping sauce and may include egg or wheat in the noodle binding. A plain tea-soba or vegetable item might be possible but would need to be confirmed in person; assume animal-based dashi by default.
kz_buemon.hours_raw: Daytime soba cafe (Buemon): 11:30-16:00. Evening soba bar (Otoyu): 18:30-01:00, closed Sun & Mon (open Sun if Mon is a holiday).
kz_buemon.notes: [Mom & Pop] Buemon occupies a renovated townhouse in a back alley of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The building was once the private residence of the proprietor of 'Toyu' (東湯), a public bathhouse that the district's geiko once frequented. It has been modernized while keeping the

chef_bio.background: Buemon occupies a renovated townhouse in a back alley of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The building was once the private residence of the proprietor of 'Toyu' (東湯), a public bathhouse that the district's geisha once frequented. It has been modernized while keeping the chic character of the chaya district, with an open counter for solo diners and a courtyard garden visible through large glass windows.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on hometown ingredients and Kanazawa's food culture, expressed through the marriage of soba with local Kaga roasted tea.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-made soba, with the signature 'Kaga-bocha soba' (加賀棒茶そば, around 880 yen) made by kneading powdered Kaga roasted tea into fine sarashina-flour noodles (the flour deliberately mutes the soba aroma to let the roasted-tea fragrance come through); it is recommended eaten first with Noto salt. By day it is a soba cafe; in the evening it runs as a soba bar (音ゆ).

anecdotes.text: The soba chef, Michihata, is a son of the owner of the 'Toyu' bathhouse; he was involved in launching several soba shops in Tokyo before returning home to open Buemon.
The signature Kaga-bocha soba was born from trial and error: the chef gathered roasted teas from across Kanazawa and repeatedly experimented before arriving at this dish.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ことりっぷ及び検索で、そばを打つのは『東湯』主人の息子・道端さん、東京で複数の蕎麦店立ち上げに関与後帰郷、更科粉に加賀棒茶を練り込んだ加賀棒茶そば(880円)を確認。higashiyu.comで昼は蕎麦・夜は蕎麦BAR音ゆ(株式会社東湯)を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a soba (buckwheat) shop whose noodles are blended with sarashina flour and roasted-tea powder; wheat is standard in soba dough and in the dipping sauce. No gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soba is served with a traditional soy-sauce-and-dashi tsuyu, which is normally wheat-based; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Traditional soba tsuyu is based on katsuobushi/animal dashi; no vegan dashi or menu is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, modern soba cafe in a renovated townhouse where a friendly greeting and pointing at the photo menu will get you by, though staff may have limited English.

kz_taisho_roman_kissa_kingy.gf_detail: This is a classic kissaten built around hot cakes, homemade pudding and other flour-, egg- and dairy-based sweets, with no gluten-free menu or allergy program documented. The signature white hot cakes are wheat pancakes. Not suitable for celiac diners; there is no dedicated gluten-free preparation.
kz_taisho_roman_kissa_kingy.vegan_detail: The menu centers on egg- and dairy-rich sweets (custard pudding with strong egg flavor, hot cakes with honey and butter, cream sodas with ice cream). No vegan options are documented. Some drinks such as plain coffee or the jelly/fruit punch may be incidentally plant-based, but you would need to ask; this is not a vegan-friendly destination.
kz_taisho_roman_kissa_kingy.hours_raw: 11:00-17:00 (L.O. 16:30); food service until around 14:00. Closed on the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays of the month.
kz_taisho_roman_kissa_kingy.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kingyoan opened in September 2022 inside a renovated Kanazawa machiya more than a century old, tucked just off the main lane of the Higashi Chaya District. The whole cafe is built as a 'time machine' back to Japan's Taisho era (1912-1926), when Western culture was first taking ro

chef_bio.origin: The name 金魚庵 (Kingyoan, 'goldfish retreat') is drawn from the goldfish that appears in Kanazawa-born novelist Muro Saisei's novel 蜜のあわれ (Mitsu no Aware); goldfish motifs are hidden throughout the interior like a treasure hunt, and hanging goldfish lamps mark the vermillion lattice entrance.
chef_bio.background: Kingyoan opened on September 9, 2022 inside a renovated Kanazawa machiya more than a century old, tucked just off the main lane of the Higashi Chaya District. The whole cafe is built as a 'time machine' back to Japan's Taisho era (1912-1926), when Western culture was first taking root: red carpets, a phonograph, a period refrigerator, stained glass and antique furnishings fill the rooms, and staff serve in kimono with frilly aprons.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe recreates Meiji- and Taisho-era recipes and decor to let guests step back in time and experience the romance of early-modern Japan.
chef_bio.specialty: Signature items include cream soda served in goldfish-bowl-shaped glasses; the summer-only goldfish-bowl soda whose decorations mimic water plants and bubbles; Haikara Punch, a colorful jelly-and-fruit soda (~800 yen); a dense old-fashioned homemade pudding with strong egg flavor and bitter caramel (~600 yen); and pale 'white' hot cakes recreated from a Taisho-era recipe using honey instead of sugar (~880 yen).

anecdotes.text: Cream sodas are served in goldfish-bowl-shaped glasses, and the summer-limited goldfish soda is designed so that, viewed from above, the bubbles and grass-like decorations resemble a real goldfish bowl.

The building is a 100-plus-year-old machiya preserved with Taisho-era furnishings, and the cafe doubles as a photography studio that can be rented (around 3,300 yen/hour) after hours and on closed days.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ことりっぷ・金沢経済新聞・ishimoで、2022年9月9日開業、築100年超の町家、大正ロマンのタイムスリップ喫茶、店名は室生犀星の小説『蜜のあわれ』の金魚に由来、金魚鉢グラスのクリームソーダ、ハイカラポンチ、自家製プリン、白いホットケーキ、撮影スタジオ貸出を確認。

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming themed cafe popular with tourists where a smile and a few words of Japanese go a long way; staff are used to visitors but English menus or fluent English service are not guaranteed.

kz_itaru_honten.gf_detail: This is a classic Japanese izakaya built around soy sauce, miso, and bonito/kombu dashi, with sashimi served with wheat-based soy sauce and many fried items (tempura, fried white shrimp). There is no documented gluten-free menu or allergen handling, so it is not safe for celiacs.
kz_itaru_honten.vegan_detail: The kitchen is centered on Sea-of-Japan seafood (sashimi platters, nodoguro, crab, yellowtail) with dashi and seafood used throughout. While some Kaga-vegetable dishes exist, they are typically prepared with dashi or other animal products, and there is no documented vegan menu.
kz_itaru_honten.hours_raw: 17:30–23:30 (L.O. 23:00); closed Sundays (and the following Monday when Sunday is a national holiday)
kz_itaru_honten.notes: Founded in 1988 in the Kakinokibatake quarter near Kanazawa's Katamachi district, Itaru grew from a neighborhood spot into what locals call one of Kanazawa's defining izakaya, especially after the Hokuriku Shinkansen reached the city in 2015 brought a wave of visitors alongside i

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1988 in the Kakinokibatake quarter near Kanazawa's Katamachi district, Itaru grew from a neighborhood spot into what locals call one of Kanazawa's defining izakaya, holding its loyal regulars even as the Hokuriku Shinkansen's 2015 arrival brought a wave of visitors.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant builds its menu around top local ingredients — day-boat fish from Toyama's Shinminato and Noto, and Kaga vegetables such as Gorojima-kintoki sweet potato, kinjiso red amaranth, Kaga futo-kyuri cucumber, and Noto taro — with chefs cooking in full view of the counter so guests can watch the craft.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the kioke-mori otsukuri — a generous sashimi platter heaped in a wooden barrel with bold seasonal cuts of Sea-of-Japan fish. Salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) is another must-order. Winter brings yopparai-gani (sake-marinated kobako crab) and kan-buri (cold-season yellowtail).

anecdotes.text: Itaru pours Tengu-mai sake drawn straight from a brewery mini-tank without bottling, a kura-dashi pour the shop describes as available nowhere else.
The counter is set up as a live-cooking stage where the head chef works alongside apprentices in front of diners; the shop is named after master Itaru himself.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon及びkanazawa.ccで、1988年創業、柿木畠、店主・石黒格(いたる)、木桶盛りのお造り、ノドグロ、天狗舞の蔵出しミニタンク、加賀野菜(五郎島金時・金時草・加賀太きゅうり・能登里芋)、新湊/能登の地魚、酔っ払い蟹・寒鰤を確認。なめろう・しめ鯖は未確認のため削除。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu relies on soy sauce, miso, and dashi with fried items (tempura, fried white shrimp) sharing the kitchen; no gluten-free accommodation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sashimi and izakaya dishes are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Seafood and dashi are central to nearly every dish; vegetable preparations are typically dashi-based.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, hugely popular local izakaya where a few words of Japanese and a reservation go a long way; counter seats let you watch the chefs, but service is fast-paced and not heavily English-oriented.

kz_kadocho_yokoanjemachi_te.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core menu is wheat udon and soba (buckwheat is typically blended with wheat flour) served in a soy-and-dashi broth, plus fried dishes (tempura, katsu). There is no indication of gluten-free options or any allergen handling, so this is not safe for celiacs.
kz_kadocho_yokoanjemachi_te.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Broths are made with fish/bonito dashi, and signature plates include saba (mackerel) miso, tempura rice bowls, ramen, and katsu. No documented vegan options.
kz_kadocho_yokoanjemachi_te.notes: [Mom & Pop] An old-school Kanazawa soba and udon shokudō tucked into the Yokoanjemachi shopping street, on the walking route between Kanazawa Station and Ōmichō Market. It has the calm, lived-in feel of a Shōwa-era neighborhood diner, serving home-style set meals at lunchtime prices that loc

chef_bio.background: An old-school Kanazawa soba and udon shokudō tucked into the Yokoanjemachi shopping street, on the walking route between Kanazawa Station and Ōmichō Market. It has the calm, lived-in feel of a Shōwa-era neighborhood diner, serving home-style set meals at lunchtime prices that locals have long relied on.
chef_bio.philosophy: Warm, home-style cooking in an unhurried, settled atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Sweet-broth udon and soba alongside hearty teishoku (set meals) — diners single out the saba miso-ni teishoku (mackerel simmered in miso), and the menu also features hayashi katsu rice, tempura egg rice bowls (ten-toji-don), ramen, and nabeyaki-udon.

anecdotes.text: Described as a 'warmhearted set-meal restaurant' offering traditional Kanazawa flavors and home-style, comforting food in a calm atmosphere, with the saba miso-ni teishoku singled out for its firm seasoning and never-tiring deliciousness.
A Shōwa-era cafeteria-style shop with a retro exterior and about 47 seats, offering soba, udon, curry, ramen and rice bowls at under ~1,000 yen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Retty・食べログ・ぐるなびで、横安江町の昭和レトロなそば・うどん定食処(約47席)、鯖味噌煮定食、ハヤシカツライス、天とじ丼、ラーメン、鍋やきうどん、落ち着いた家庭的な雰囲気を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat udon and soba share kitchen and likely boiling water; fried items (tempura, katsu) use wheat batter/breading. No allergen separation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy-sauce-and-dashi broths are used throughout; conventional soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths rely on fish/bonito dashi and the menu centers on fish, egg, and meat dishes; no vegan preparation is indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills local lunch spot with no English menu or English-speaking staff expected, so a foreign student is best off going with a guide or someone who reads Japanese.

kz_uouma.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a sushi and seafood-bowl counter built around vinegared rice served with house sushi soy sauce (blended on a Kanazawa Ohno shoyu base), plus typical accompaniments like tamagoyaki — all wheat-containing. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergy program. Not safe for celiacs.
kz_uouma.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is fresh local seafood — sashimi bowls and nigiri. The signature dish is a 12-topping all-seafood kaisendon. No plant-based options are documented.
kz_uouma.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00 (approx.); irregular closures, some sources note closed Wed.
kz_uouma.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner comes from an established sushi-restaurant background and personally selects the fish, bringing a trained sushi craftsman's eye to a casual market counter in the heart of Omicho Market.

chef_bio.background: The owner comes from an established (老舗) sushi-restaurant background and personally selects the fish, bringing a trained sushi craftsman's eye to a casual market counter in the heart of Omicho Market.
chef_bio.philosophy: A committed local-production, local-consumption ethos: Oku-Noto Koshihikari rice cooked with Hakusan spring water, blended with pure rice vinegar from the old Tsurugi town, and finished with a house sushi soy sauce built on Kanazawa Ohno shoyu — rice, vinegar, water and soy sauce all sourced locally for a balanced bite.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the 魚旨丼 kaisendon (around 2,480 yen) piled with twelve different all-seafood toppings in thick-cut slices, served over mild, lightly-tart vinegared rice meant to bring out the natural sweetness of the fish. Hand-pressed nigiri of seasonal local fish and the owner's own tamagoyaki round out the menu.

anecdotes.text: The shop leans into a homey, welcoming feel and has built a loyal following of both tourists and locals who return for the generously heaped seafood bowls.
Every element of the rice is deliberately local — Oku-Noto Koshihikari cooked with Hakusan spring water, Tsurugi-town pure rice vinegar, and a Kanazawa Ohno shoyu-based sushi soy.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 近江町市場公式・週末金沢で、老舗寿司店出身の店主が目利き、12種盛りの魚旨丼(2,480円)、奥能登コシヒカリ・白山伏流水・鶴来の純米酢・大野醤油ベースの寿司醤油という地元素材、自家製玉子焼き、観光客と地元客の常連を確認。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: House sushi soy sauce is blended on a Kanazawa Ohno shoyu base; conventional Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly market counter where pointing at the photo menu and a cheerful greeting will carry you through; little to no English, but the staff are noted as warm and attentive.

kz_oden_yoshibou.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Oden is simmered in a soy-sauce-and-dashi broth, and many ingredients (fish cakes/hanpen, chikuwa, ganmodoki, fried tofu) contain or are bound with wheat. The signature dishes lean on soy sauce and fish dashi. No gluten-free menu or allowance is documented, and the kitchen is not celiac-safe.
kz_oden_yoshibou.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is a fish/seafood dashi, signature items include bai-gai (whelk) simmered whole in the stock and local fish dishes, and most oden ingredients sit in the same animal-based pot. No vegan menu or preparation is documented.
kz_oden_yoshibou.hours_raw: 17:30-21:30. Closed Sundays; holidays are an irregular closure.
kz_oden_yoshibou.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yoshibou is a long-running Kanazawa oden shop in the Kōrinbō district. It first opened in 1957, and after the previous owner passed away the shop went quiet for a time before the family revived it; today it is carried on by proprietress Yoshie Koshida together with her son Kōta,

chef_bio.chef_name: Yoshie Koshida (越田良枝) and her son Kōta (皓太)
chef_bio.background: Yoshibou is a long-running Kanazawa oden shop in the Kōrinbō district. It first opened in 1957, and after the previous owner passed away the shop went quiet for a time before the family revived it, continuing an roughly 70-year legacy; today it is carried on by proprietress Yoshie Koshida together with her son Kōta (the third generation), who set a warm counter atmosphere favored by locals and people on work assignment in the city.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen measures the salinity of the broth daily and adjusts the seasoning to the weather and temperature, aiming for a stock with lingering, deep flavor. The cooking avoids chemical seasonings in favor of a gentle, ingredient-forward taste, and the shop is a member of the Kanazawa Oden veteran-shops association (金沢おでん老舗50年会).
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa-style oden simmered in a light, local dashi built on bonito, kombu, Kanazawa soy sauce, sake and salt. A signature is bai-gai (whelk) simmered whole in the broth and shucked to order, prized for its briny aroma; the shop is also known for obanzai side dishes and a sake list chosen to match the food.

anecdotes.text: The shop opened in 1957 and, after the previous owner passed away over a decade ago, was revived by the family's son, returning Yoshibou's oden to its longtime Kōrinbō spot.
Proprietress Yoshie Koshida and her son Kōta run the counter together, creating the warm, gentle-flavored atmosphere the shop is known for.
The broth is kept gentle and free of chemical seasonings; salinity is measured daily and tuned to the day's climate, and bai-gai (whelk), a Kanazawa oden specialty, is served from the pot.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 食べログ・金沢日和・観光協会・検索で、昭和32年(1957)創業、先代逝去後に息子が復活させ約70年続く、女将・越田良枝と息子・皓太(3代目)、化学調味料不使用の優しい味、日々塩分濃度を計測、ばい貝、金沢おでん老舗50年会所属を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Oden is cooked communally in a single soy-sauce-and-dashi pot containing wheat-based items such as fish cakes, chikuwa and fried tofu, so heavy cross-contact with gluten is inherent to the dish.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-sauce-based dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the broth and most simmered items are not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shared simmering broth is a fish/seafood dashi and includes seafood such as whole bai-gai (whelk), so vegan separation is not possible.

positives.text: Cooking avoids chemical seasonings, with broth salinity measured daily and seasoning adjusted to the day's conditions for a gentle, ingredient-forward taste.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally loved counter oden shop where some basic Japanese and pointing at the simmering pot will help; an English menu is not documented, so come open to a little adventure.

kz_daikoku_sushi.gf_detail: This is a traditional sushi counter where soy sauce (typically wheat-containing) is central and dishes rely on standard sushi seasonings; there is no indication of gluten-free accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_daikoku_sushi.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused sushi house built around Hokuriku fish (nodoguro, white shrimp, anago). There is no documented vegan offering; even rice and broths likely involve fish-based dashi. Not suitable for vegans.
kz_daikoku_sushi.hours_raw: Mon-Tue, Thu-Sat: 11:00-13:30 and 17:00-19:00; Sun: 11:00-13:30 (lunch only, no dinner); Wed: closed. (Some listings show slightly later dinner end around 19:30.)
kz_daikoku_sushi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, tucked-away counter sushi shop just outside Omichō Market at the Jukkenmachi exit, where the master forms each piece by hand at the counter while the front-of-house hostess attends to guests in a calm, unhurried room.

roles: Itamae (master sushi chef) at the counter
Okami-san (hostess) handling the front of house
chef_bio.background: A small, tucked-away counter sushi shop just outside Omichō Market at the Jukkenmachi exit, with about ten counter seats, where the master forms each piece by hand while the front-of-house hostess (his wife) attends to guests in a calm, unhurried room.
chef_bio.philosophy: Sushi made to the diner's pace: the master shapes and serves the pieces one at a time as you eat, so each arrives fresh from his hands.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-formed nigiri showcasing Hokuriku seafood — seared nodoguro (rosy seabass), white shrimp (shiroebi), anago and seasonal local fish. A seasonal omakase course pairs about a dozen pieces of nigiri with a roll and soup, praised as strong value.

anecdotes.text: The master hand-forms each piece at the counter while the okami carefully presents the dishes, giving the room a calm, personal feel.
The omakase course of about twelve nigiri plus a roll and soup is praised as outstanding value, with seared nodoguro and white shrimp as highlights.
Sushi is served one piece at a time, paced to how quickly the diner eats, so each piece is freshly made.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Retty・食べログで、近江町市場十間町口の10席の小さなカウンター店、大将と女将さん、炙りノドグロ・白えび・穴子、約12貫のお任せ+汁物、一皿ずつ客のペースで提供を確認。『梅』コース名と甘えびは未確認のため削除。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a traditional sushi counter, soy sauce (typically brewed with wheat) is used throughout; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is built entirely around fish and shellfish (nodoguro, white shrimp, anago); broths and rice seasoning likely include fish-based ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny traditional counter sushi shop run by an older master and front-of-house hostess; little to no English is likely, so basic Japanese or a translation app and a phone reservation will make your visit smooth.

kz_korinbo_rakuya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The house specialty jibuni (治部煮) is made by dusting duck/chicken in wheat flour and simmering it with Kanazawa fu (wheat gluten) in a wheat-soy-sauce-based broth, and the izakaya menu relies on soy sauce and dashi throughout. There is no indication of gluten-free accommodation, so it is not celiac-safe.
kz_korinbo_rakuya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. This is a Kaga-cuisine izakaya built around fresh Hokuriku seafood, duck/chicken jibuni, and bonito/kombu dashi. No vegan menu or documented plant-based accommodation; vegans would have very little to eat.
kz_korinbo_rakuya.hours_raw: Mon–Sat & day before public holidays: Lunch 11:30–13:30 (food L.O. 13:30); Dinner 17:00–22:00 (food L.O. 21:00). Closed Sundays and public holidays.
kz_korinbo_rakuya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Korinbo Rakuya is a Kanazawa machiya (traditional townhouse) izakaya tucked into the central Korinbo district, where the weathered wooden architecture, tatami zashiki rooms and a serene inner garden give it the feel of an old Kanazawa merchant's home. It is one of the comparative

chef_bio.background: Korinbo Rakuya is a Kanazawa machiya (traditional townhouse) izakaya tucked into the central Korinbo district, where the weathered wooden architecture, tatami zashiki rooms and a serene inner garden give it the feel of an old Kanazawa merchant's home. It is one of the comparatively few local spots where you can order Kaga regional dishes individually rather than only as part of a set course.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature dish is jibuni (治部煮), the classic Kaga stew of wheat-flour-dusted duck simmered with Kanazawa's fu (wheat gluten) and seasonal vegetables in a glossy thickened broth, finished with a sharp dab of wasabi. Rakuya is noted for serving jibuni as an affordable single à-la-carte plate, alongside seasonal Hokuriku seafood and Kaga vegetables paired with local sake.

anecdotes.text: The menu centers on Ishikawa seafood, Kaga vegetables and local sake served amid the atmosphere of a Kanazawa machiya townhouse, with a tatami room looking onto an inner garden.
Diners can enjoy jibuni featuring duck, Kanazawa fu, a distinctive broth and wasabi offered as an inexpensive single dish, a relatively rare way to sample the dish in the city.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 食べログ(英)・ヒトサラで、香林坊の町家居酒屋、座敷と内庭、治部煮(鴨・麩・わさび)を安価な単品で提供(市内では稀)、石川の海鮮・加賀野菜・地酒を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature jibuni is made with wheat-flour-coated meat and wheat-gluten fu in a soy-sauce broth, so gluten is integral to the kitchen and the menu is not suitable for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kaga cuisine such as jibuni is built on wheat-containing soy sauce and dashi; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is centered on seafood, duck/chicken and bonito/kombu dashi, so plant-only dishes cannot be assumed free of animal-based broth.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional Kanazawa machiya izakaya where staff likely speak limited English, so a few basic Japanese phrases and pointing at the menu will help a foreign student feel at ease.

kz_sabo_soshin.gf_detail: This is a traditional sweets cafe whose menu centers on wheat- and dairy-based items: cheesecake, parfaits, Japanese confections (wagashi/上生菓子), and zenzai. There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and no allergen handling described. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_sabo_soshin.vegan_detail: Plant-based options are not advertised. Plain matcha, hojicha, and brewed coffee/tea are likely vegan as drinks, but the sweets (parfaits, cheesecake, wagashi, zenzai) typically contain dairy, eggs, or refined ingredients. Kakigori syrups may be acceptable but ice/sweets are not verified vegan. A vegan diner would need to ask in person and limit to plain beverages.
kz_sabo_soshin.hours_raw: 10:00 until varies (closing time changes day to day). Closed Wed (with occasional irregular closures). Guests are asked to order at least one item per person.
kz_sabo_soshin.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independent tea-and-sweets cafe that has quietly operated for over a decade (around 13 years as of the mid-2020s), set inside a renovated traditional townhouse (machiya) right on the main street of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The owners describe their aim s

chef_bio.origin: 金沢・東山（ひがし茶屋街）
chef_bio.background: A small, independent tea-and-sweets cafe that has quietly operated for over a decade (around 13 years as of the mid-2020s), set inside a renovated traditional townhouse (machiya) on the main street of Kanazawa's Higashi Chaya geisha district. The owners describe their aim simply: to keep the spirit of an old-fashioned kissaten (Japanese coffeehouse) alive, refining the craft day by day.
chef_bio.philosophy: Doing the simple things carefully — grinding and brewing each cup of coffee by hand, and preserving the calm, unhurried feel of a classic neighborhood coffeehouse rather than chasing trends.
chef_bio.specialty: Cup-by-cup hand-brewed coffee and Viennese coffee; matcha and hojicha parfaits; cheesecake; zenzai (sweet red-bean soup); premium seasonal wagashi (上生菓子); and, in summer, around eight kinds of Japanese-style kakigori (shaved ice, ~900 yen) served with the ice and syrup separate so guests sweeten to taste.

anecdotes.text: The shop sums up its own ethos as 'in our 13th year, striving daily to be an old-fashioned coffeehouse.'
The renovated machiya has counter seats on the first floor and, on the second, window seats that look out over the historic Higashi Chaya streetscape — a favorite rest stop between sightseeing.

In summer the cafe serves about eight varieties of Japanese kakigori (black sesame, matcha, strawberry-and-cream, mango, Kaga hojicha, kinako-kuromitsu, yuzu, strawberry) at around 900 yen, with the shaved ice and syrup brought separately so you can adjust the sweetness yourself.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ぐるなび・金沢ラボ・金沢日和で、『創業13年、昔ながらの喫茶店を目指して』のコンセプト、1杯ずつ豆を挽くコーヒー、ウィンナーコーヒー、抹茶/ほうじ茶パフェ、チーズケーキ、ぜんざい、上生菓子、2階の窓席、夏の8種の和かき氷(約900円、氷とシロップ別)を確認。『石臼挽き』は裏付けが取れず削除。

positives.text: Kakigori is served with the ice and syrup separate, so guests can control sweetness and see what they are adding.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, tourist-friendly old-townhouse tea cafe where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the sweets menu will get you a warm welcome, but plan to order at least one item per person as the shop requests.

kz_tsuchiya.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The café serves wagashi and toast-style items with no celiac protocols documented; the complimentary sweets are chosen by the house. No dedicated equipment or allergen handling is described, so it is not suitable for someone needing strict gluten avoidance.
kz_tsuchiya.vegan_detail: No vegan menu is advertised. The core offering is coffee and seasonal wagashi (Japanese sweets such as yokan, zenzai/sweet red-bean soup, wasanbon-sugar items); many wagashi are plant-based, but ingredients (e.g. dairy in some items, sweets served as a complimentary set you cannot choose) are not specified. A vegan visitor would need to ask in Japanese about each item.
kz_tsuchiya.hours_raw: Listings vary: standard listing shows 10:00–17:00, closed Mon & Tue. A 2023 update reports a change (from Aug 2023) to weekends/holidays only — Sat & Sun 11:00–18:00, holidays 11:00–17:00. Irregular closures noted.
kz_tsuchiya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Tsuchiya occupies a wooden townhouse built in 1913 (Taisho 2) in Kazuemachi, one of Kanazawa's historic teahouse districts, on the banks of the Asano River between the Asanogawa-ohashi and Nakano-bashi bridges. chef_bio.background: Tsuchiya occupies a wooden townhouse built in 1913 (Taisho 2) in Kazuemachi, one of Kanazawa's historic teahouse districts, on the banks of the Asano River between the Asanogawa-ohashi and Nakano-bashi bridges. The building is a Kanazawa-registered traditional structure, recognizable by its deep red bengara-pigment walls. It has been converted into a small café that keeps the spirit of the old chaya intact.
chef_bio.philosophy: A quiet, gracious tea-time: guests are welcomed with complimentary tea and a seasonal sweet while their order is prepared, and the second-floor tatami room is dressed with seasonal hanging scrolls and alcove crafts reflecting Kanazawa's four seasons.
chef_bio.specialty: House 'Tsuchiya coffee' (about 500 yen) and Vietnamese Dalat coffee, each accompanied by seasonal wagashi; seasonal specialties include wasanbon iced coffee in summer and zenzai (sweet red-bean soup) in winter, served on Wajima lacquerware.

anecdotes.text: The large second-floor windows frame the cherry-lined Asano River so closely that blossoms feel within reach in spring, while in winter white migratory birds gather on the water below.
Reviewers single out the value: a modestly priced coffee comes with included sweets and a serene riverside view from the old tatami room.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ことりっぷ・フォートラベルで、大正2年(1913)築の主計町の町家、浅野川沿い(浅野川大橋〜中の橋)、市指定保存建造物、紅殻塗りの朱壁、土家コーヒー(約500円)、ダラットコーヒー、和三盆アイスコーヒー/ぜんざい、輪島塗、ウェルカムのお茶と菓子、2階座敷の川景色を確認。

positives.text: Coffee is paired with seasonal Japanese sweets like yokan and zenzai, several of which are traditionally plant-based, though the specific items are chosen by the house and not selectable.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run townhouse café where service is in Japanese with little English; lovely but best approached with a phrasebook or a Japanese-speaking friend, and patience for irregular opening days.

kz_kanazawa_oden_to_obanzai.gf_detail: A Kanazawa oden and obanzai izakaya. The cuisine is built on dashi (typically fish/kelp/soy-based broth), soy sauce, and wheat-based ingredients — Kanazawa oden famously includes 車麩 (wheel-shaped wheat gluten) and many simmered items soaked in soy-flavored broth. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_kanazawa_oden_to_obanzai.vegan_detail: This is a seafood-and-meat-forward izakaya specializing in Kanazawa oden, obanzai, karaage and mapo tofu, with dashi-based broths throughout. Obanzai (seasonal home-style vegetable side dishes) may include some plant-based items, but almost all are prepared with fish dashi and soy seasoning, so they are not reliably vegan. No documented vegan menu or accommodation; a vegan would need to ask and options would be minimal.
kz_kanazawa_oden_to_obanzai.hours_raw: Tabelog: Mon-Tue, Thu-Sun & holidays 20:00-03:00 (Food L.O. 02:00, Drinks L.O. 02:30); closed Wednesdays. Official site frames it as dinner from 18:00 with a late-night bar continuing afterward.
kz_kanazawa_oden_to_obanzai.notes: [Mom & Pop] さんさん is a small, late-night oden-and-obanzai izakaya tucked on the third floor of a building in Katamachi, the heart of Kanazawa's Korinbo-Katamachi nightlife district. A relatively recent arrival to the scene, it sets out to offer 'local flavors and drinks enjoyed casually at a

roles: 金沢おでん・おばんざいの居酒屋
chef_bio.background: さんさん is a small, late-night oden-and-obanzai izakaya on the third floor of a building in Katamachi, the heart of Kanazawa's Korinbo-Katamachi nightlife district. A relatively recent arrival to the scene, it sets out to offer 'local flavors and drinks enjoyed casually at a bar,' with counter seats designed so that solo guests can drop in comfortably.
chef_bio.philosophy: A relaxed neighborhood spot pairing Kanazawa's home-cooking traditions with easygoing late-night drinking, welcoming everyone from solo diners to groups.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa oden simmered in a regional broth (including local touches like 車麩 wheel-shaped wheat gluten and 赤巻き red-swirl kamaboko), a daily-changing platter of obanzai home-style side dishes built around seasonal ingredients, plus casual izakaya small plates. By the late hours it shifts into bar mode, known for its tea-based shochu highballs alongside sake and cocktails.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen leans into Kanazawa oden's signature local ingredients and rotates its obanzai daily with the season, while the late-night counter is built around tea-infused shochu highballs that are something of a house specialty.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト・ヒトサラで、片町3階の金沢おでん・おばんざい酒場、車麩や赤巻き入りの金沢おでん、日替わりおばんざい、緑茶/ジャスミン等の茶割り焼酎ハイボール、一人客歓迎のカウンター、深夜のバー営業を確認。唐揚げ・麻婆豆腐は未確認のため一般表現に変更。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Kanazawa oden is built on soy-and-dashi broth and includes wheat-based items such as 車麩 (wheel-shaped wheat gluten); fried items like karaage are wheat-battered, so shared broth and fryer cross-contact should be assumed.
gf_cross_contamination.source_wording: 「金沢おでんは、地元ならではの食材を使ったご当地グルメです。車麩や赤巻きといった特徴的な具材が入り、だしの旨みがしっかり染み込んでいます。金沢ならではの味わいをお楽しみください！」

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The menu centers on oden and obanzai seasoned with soy sauce and dashi, which in Japan are virtually always wheat-containing; no wheat-free seasoning is documented.
soy_sauce_wheat.source_wording: 「名物の金沢おでんやおばんざいをはじめ、旬の食材を活かした一品料理が自慢です。」／「車麩や赤巻きといった特徴的な具材が入り、だしの旨みがしっかり染み込んでいます。」

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths and obanzai are typically made with fish dashi and the menu features karaage, mapo tofu and seafood, so vegetable dishes likely share animal-based broth and preparation surfaces.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, late-night local izakaya where you order in Japanese and there is no documented English support, so it is most comfortable if you can manage basic Japanese or come with a Japanese-speaking friend.

kz_salon_de_the_kawamura.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The menu centers on Japanese sweets; while items like warabi mochi (bracken starch) and amanatto (candied beans) can be naturally wheat-free, the café also serves wagashi and dessert items that may contain or be cross-contacted with wheat, and no gluten-free protocol is documented. A celiac visitor would need to ask carefully about each item.
kz_salon_de_the_kawamura.vegan_detail: Several plant-based-leaning sweets exist: warabi mochi served with kinako (soybean flour) and kuromitsu (black sugar syrup), amanatto (candied beans), yokan, and bean-based jellies and parfait layers are typically dairy-free. However, parfaits and kakigori include ice cream and condensed milk, and some shiratama/dessert components may use dairy. Vegan items are available but not guaranteed; confirm dairy-free options when ordering.
kz_salon_de_the_kawamura.hours_raw: Weekdays (Mon–Sat) 10:00–17:30 (L.O. 17:00); Sundays & holidays 10:00–16:30 (L.O. 16:00). Entry ages 6 and up; one order minimum per person.
kz_salon_de_the_kawamura.notes: Salon de The Kawamura is the second-floor tea salon above 甘納豆かわむら (Amanatto Kawamura), a specialty shop in Kanazawa's Nishi Chaya geisha district devoted to amanatto — candied azuki and other beans — along with yokan and jelly confections. The salon was created so visitors can si

chef_bio.background: Salon de The Kawamura is the second-floor tea salon above 甘納豆かわむら (Amanatto Kawamura), a specialty shop in Kanazawa's Nishi Chaya geisha district devoted to amanatto — candied azuki and other beans — along with yokan and jelly confections. The salon was created so visitors can sit and savor the same carefully sourced ingredients freshly made on the premises, with large windows looking out over the historic Nishi Chaya streetscape.
chef_bio.philosophy: The salon is conceived as a quiet, serene space (静寂なる空間) emphasizing freshly made sweets from carefully selected ingredients, with the bean as the protagonist of each dish.
chef_bio.specialty: Signature offerings include a Kawamura parfait layering the shop's red beans with matcha, Kaga bo-cha (hojicha), apricot, mascarpone and soy elements; warabi mochi made with genuine domestic bracken starch served with house-made kuromitsu from Hateruma Island (波照間島) black sugar; and seasonal kakigori such as a hojicha shaved ice with house-made red bean paste, plus a matcha version, alongside strawberry preparations that use local tofu shiratama from a neighborhood tofu maker.

anecdotes.text: The salon admits guests aged 6 and older, asks for one order per person, and notes that its handmade sweets require preparation time — a deliberate framing of the experience as an unhurried, grown-up tea break.
The hojicha kakigori (around 1,100 yen) hides hojicha ice cream inside the shaved ice and is finished with house-made red bean paste and large beans.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 食べ物系サイト(food-japon)と公式店舗情報(mame-kawamura.com)は2階サロンの入店年齢6才以上・一人一品・作りたてを、かき氷ブログ(momoclobiyori)はほうじ茶かき氷(自家製あん・ほうじ茶アイス)を確認。

vegan_cross_contact.text: Parfaits and kakigori include ice cream and condensed milk, so shared scoops and prep surfaces could contact dairy even on otherwise plant-based bean and warabi items.

positives.text: Warabi mochi is served with kinako (soybean flour) and kuromitsu (black sugar syrup), and amanatto, yokan and bean jellies are typically dairy-free options for plant-based guests.

cultural_comfort.note: A serene Japanese tea salon where a few words of Japanese and patience help, since handmade desserts take time and English support is limited; note children under 6 are not admitted.

kz_kanazawa_washoku_minna_n.gf_detail: A traditional Kanazawa washoku spot built around dashi, soy sauce, sake and fried/simmered dishes (e.g. crab cream croquette, beef tendon stew). No gluten-free menu or handling is documented, and wheat-based soy sauce is central to Japanese cooking here — not suitable for celiacs.
kz_kanazawa_washoku_minna_n.vegan_detail: The menu centers on fresh fish (daily-sourced sashimi, nodoguro), seafood, and meat dishes, with dashi-based seasoning throughout. No vegan or vegetarian options are advertised; this is a seafood- and meat-forward Kaga washoku restaurant.
kz_kanazawa_washoku_minna_n.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 17:00-00:00 (food L.O. 23:00, drinks L.O. 23:30). Closed Sun.
kz_kanazawa_washoku_minna_n.notes: [Mom & Pop] Chef Manabu Maeda trained for about ten years at the well-regarded kappo restaurant Takeshi, then worked at a fresh-fish shop before going independent and opening his own place in August 2018. The shop's name, 'Minna no Manabu' (everyone's Manabu), reflects its friendly, unpreten

chef_bio.background: Chef Manabu Maeda trained for about ten years at the well-regarded kappo restaurant Takeshi (割烹たけし), where innovative Japanese cooking won over an aspiring Western-food cook, then worked at a fresh-fish shop to master fish and knife work before going independent and opening his own place in August 2018. The shop's name, 'Minna no Manabu' (everyone's Manabu), reflects its friendly, unpretentious spirit.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcase fresh local Kanazawa and Kaga ingredients in honest, well-crafted Japanese cooking at accessible prices, served in a relaxed, welcoming atmosphere rather than a formal high-end setting.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily-sourced sashimi platters with six or seven varieties of fish, salt-grilled nodoguro (rosy seabass), and a much-loved beef tendon stew — the overwhelming bestseller — simmered two to three hours in a salt-based broth; seasonal Kaga vegetables and winter kobako crab also feature.

anecdotes.text: Maeda spent roughly a decade honing his craft at the popular kappo restaurant Takeshi, then worked at a fishmonger's before opening his own restaurant in August 2018 — experience that shows in the morning-fresh fish sourced daily from a trusted local fish vendor.
The kitchen brings contemporary plating to traditional Japanese techniques and leans on Kaga vegetables, pairing dishes with highballs and locally made Kaga plum wine.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ヒトサラの料理人紹介は前多学(1980年生・石川県出身)が割烹たけしで約10年修業→鮮魚店→2018年8月独立と記載。公式サイト(gorp)は刺身6～7種・のどぐろ・塩仕立ての牛すじ煮込み(一番人気)・貸切20席を確認。

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free handling is documented; fried dishes such as crab cream croquette are on the menu, implying shared frying and breading with wheat.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Traditional Kanazawa washoku relying on soy sauce and dashi seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and no GF substitute is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dashi (typically fish/bonito based) and fresh seafood are central to the cooking, so animal products pervade the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a warm, no-frills local izakaya-style washoku counter where some basic Japanese will help you order and chat with the chef; an English menu is not advertised, so a translation app is handy.

kz_amanatto_kawamura.gf_detail: A traditional wagashi (Japanese confectionery) maker. Many sweets like daifuku and shitatari-mochi are made from glutinous rice (mochi/gyūhi) and azuki, which can be naturally wheat-free, but yōkan, sweet beans, jellies and shared kitchen equipment mean nothing is verified gluten-free. There is no celiac protocol; ask in person about specific items before ordering. Not a dedicated gluten-free destination.
kz_amanatto_kawamura.vegan_detail: The core products are plant-based by tradition: amanatto (sugar-candied beans), yōkan, bean-paste daifuku and fruit jellies are typically made from beans, sugar, agar and rice with no animal products. However, some confections and the 2F tea salon menu may use dairy, eggs or honey, and none of this is labeled vegan. Confirm individual items in person.
kz_amanatto_kawamura.hours_raw: Shop: weekdays & Saturday 9:30-18:00; Sundays/holidays 9:00-17:00. 2F tea salon (Salon de The Kawamura): weekdays 10:00-17:00 (closes 17:30), Sundays/holidays 10:00-16:00 (closes 16:30).

chef_bio.background: Kawamura began as a wholesale bean and confectionery business in Kanazawa with a history said to stretch back roughly a century. The family opened this retail shop in the historic Nishi-Chaya geisha district in 2001, set in a traditional wooden machiya directly across from the district's old geisha registry office, and renovated it in November 2013.
chef_bio.philosophy: Handcrafted quality using local, seasonal Kanazawa ingredients, served in a calm, serene setting, with sweets made without artificial colors or preservatives even at the cost of a short shelf life.
chef_bio.specialty: Amanatto (sugar-candied beans made without artificial coloring or preservatives), alongside yōkan, seasonal fruit jellies, strawberry daifuku, and the beloved shitatari-mochi, a sweet-bean filling wrapped in gyūhi mochi so tender it seems to drip, sold with just a three-day shelf life.

anecdotes.text: The signature shitatari-mochi is named for being 'so soft it seems to drip,' and is sold with a shelf life of only three days from purchase, prioritizing freshness over longevity.

The shop sits in the Nishi-Chaya geisha quarter in a traditional machiya opposite the old kennibanshō (geisha registry office), and the founder's wife contributed the gentle, calming typeface used on the packaging.

chef_bio.background: Before opening Ageha, owner Jō Ueda spent some 40 years working at a kamaboko (fish-cake) maker that supplied traditional Japanese restaurants, rising to factory manager. After leaving, he opened this small counter shop to share what most people never taste — surimi and satsuma-age eaten the moment they are made.
chef_bio.philosophy: Ueda wants diners to discover that fish cakes and satsuma-age are not the supermarket-processed versions they know — that freshly fried surimi is something exceptional, served light, fluffy, and at its peak the instant it leaves the fryer.
chef_bio.specialty: The hugely popular lunch 'Ageha Gozen' (around 1,500 yen) brings together sashimi, just-fried satsuma-age, and seasonal seafood manju (sea urchin tofu, clam, pumpkin, sweet shrimp and more), with rice and soup, often finished with a seafood-kimchi dashi chazuke. Dinner is reservation-only chef's courses of fish-paste and seafood dishes, including an occasional 'raw kamaboko' made from fresh fish cured about a week until it sets.

anecdotes.text: Ueda spent about 40 years at a kamaboko manufacturer serving traditional restaurants, finishing as factory manager, before opening this counter-only shop of roughly nine seats to let people taste freshly made surimi directly.
The lunch 'Ageha Gozen' is so sought-after that customers regularly line up before opening, and lunch runs until it sells out.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa, Namikimachi — at the foot of Umebashi Bridge along the Asano River, near the Higashi Chaya District
chef_bio.background: A neighborhood sushi shop founded about 68 years ago and run by the same family across three generations. The name 八郎 (Hachiro, literally 'eighth son') comes from the founding grandfather, who was the eighth of twelve siblings. Today the third-generation chef shapes the sushi, having trained at the well-regarded Taihei Sushi in Nonoichi; his father, the second generation, still works the counter beside him, and his mother handles the service. It keeps the easygoing, good-natured feel of an old-fashioned Showa-era sushi shop in a neighborhood that has otherwise modernized.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing fresh local (jimono) ingredients through skilled, unpretentious craftsmanship while welcoming guests with warm, family hospitality.
chef_bio.specialty: Omakase nigiri and sushi-and-sashimi assortments built on local Ishikawa, Kaga and Noto seafood — seasonal fish, crab, and yellowtail — paired with local sake.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name comes from the first-generation founder (the chef's grandfather), who was the eighth of twelve siblings, hence 'Hachiro' — eighth son.
Three generations work together: the third-generation son shapes the sushi (after training at Taihei Sushi), the second-generation father stands at the counter, and the mother handles service.
Praised by a local writer as one of the most quintessentially Kanazawa sushi shops.
The restaurant appeared in the film 'Inochi no Teishajo' featuring Sayuri Yoshinaga.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa, with founding-family roots in the Kansai region
chef_bio.background: A family-run sushi shop in central Kanazawa's Hakuro-cho, founded around 70 years ago by the current owner's grandfather and now run by the fourth generation of the Yoshikawa family. It sits a short walk from Omicho Market, where the chef buys fish fresh each morning rather than in bulk, keeping the catch consistently fresh.
chef_bio.philosophy: Buying fish daily from Omicho Market to ensure freshness, and offering approachable, affordable sushi that keeps both locals and travelers coming back across four generations.
chef_bio.specialty: Local Kanazawa fish platters and the value-priced Ichihan lunch set (nine pieces of nigiri plus a thin roll and miso soup for around 1,100 yen, weekday lunch only). A quiet specialty is the anago (sea eel), simmered and then flame-finished (aburi) for a fragrant crust. Reflecting the family's Kansai roots, the menu also includes battera and grilled-mackerel sushi, plus a choi-nomi tasting set (around 1,650 yen) with sashimi, grilled fish, pickles and soup.

anecdotes.text: The interior walls are lined with messages and photographs left by international customers over the years, reflecting the shop's long-standing welcome to visitors from abroad.
The family's Kansai roots show up on the menu through dishes like battera (pressed mackerel sushi) and grilled-mackerel sushi.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a traditional sushi restaurant, dishes are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; this is the default and there is no documented gluten-free or wheat-free soy sauce option.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen centers on seafood from Omicho Market and dashi-based soup, so cross-contact with fish is unavoidable; no separate vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: The walls are covered with notes and photos from international visitors, an English menu is available, and the family welcomes foreign guests, so a foreign student can dine comfortably here.

chef_bio.background: Founder Junko Kobayashi worked in Ishikawa restaurants and bakeries and later as a TV and radio reporter before becoming a natural-sweets planner. While presenting at a university hospital event she was struck by how many more people live with food allergies than she had imagined, and that experience inspired her to open a bakery that people with dietary restrictions could enjoy without worry.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything is made with 100% domestic rice flour and no wheat gluten, avoiding the seven mandatory allergen ingredients and additives such as thickeners, and leavened with house-made apple yeast so that people with allergies can eat more freely. After opening she spent a full year refining the recipes.
chef_bio.specialty: 100% domestic Koshihikari rice flour bread with a crisp crust and chewy (mochi-like) interior; salt bread 'Solte', seven to eight kinds of muffins, rice flour chiffon cakes, cheesecakes and tarts, and soy-milk vegan cakes.

anecdotes.text: Kobayashi decided to open the shop after realizing at a university hospital event how many people live with food allergies, opening WAGOME in the Kanazawa station-west area in 2014 after a year of recipe development.
The shop achieves the rice-flour bread's signature 'crispy outside, chewy inside' texture using house-made apple yeast instead of gluten or additives.

chef_bio.background: Daidai opened on April 29, 2023 in Kanazawa's lively Katamachi district, just behind Korinbo Tokyu Square. The shop's whole concept is to serve the city's two great local specialties under one roof: Kanazawa curry and Hunton rice.
chef_bio.philosophy: Owner Isao Shimabukuro makes the demi-glace, tartar sauce and curry roux from scratch and refuses to cut corners, saying he simply wants delicious food to make people smile.
chef_bio.specialty: The flagship 'Daidai Hunton Rice' (around 2,000 yen) is a fluffy omurice crowned with fried white fish, tartar sauce and two oversized shrimp fries; the tartar sauce hides a note of daidai (bitter orange) - the citrus that gives the shop its name - for a refreshing finish. The other pillar is Kanazawa-style cutlet curry (around 1,400 yen), a thick, spiced dark roux over a crisp breaded cutlet and shredded cabbage, served on the classic stainless boat dish.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant's name and its signature tartar sauce both come from daidai (bitter orange), which is folded into the sauce to lift the richness of the fried shrimp and fish.
The retro, wood-toned dining room also serves local Kanazawa craft beer and a house yuzu soda alongside the food.

chef_bio.background: Cajon to Seed began life simply as "Cajon," named after the cajón — the wooden box-drum that founding members fell for at a live concert. The instrument became the shop's metaphor: different parts coming together to make one harmony. The current representative, Okada, who hails from Nomi City in Ishikawa, joined as part of that founding team roughly 18 years ago and took the reins as owner about nine years in, during a major renovation that reshaped the place into the airy, plant-filled organic café-dining it is today.
chef_bio.philosophy: Okada wants to retire the old idea that organic food has to taste dull — the kitchen chases genuinely delicious organic cooking and treats natural, additive-free eating as an everyday way to look after one's health, while respecting that diners make their own choices. The brown rice is grown pesticide-free in the restaurant's own paddies and cooked with cold Kawachi-village water kept out of direct sun; seasonings are additive-free, including products from Nakashō, a 129-year-old Ishikawa maker.
chef_bio.specialty: The weekly-changing Seed Lunch (around 1,750 yen) is the heart of the menu — a colorful plate of four seasonal dishes built around pesticide-free brown rice, an organic salad, a vegetable soup and a drink. It regularly sells out within about an hour of opening. Other favorites include the Seed Taco Rice, chicken-basil stir-fry rice, organic smoothies and fresh-pressed juices, single-origin hand-dripped coffee, and house-made muffins.

anecdotes.text: The name comes from the cajón drum that inspired the original founders at a live show — chosen to symbolize how different parts create one harmony.
The pesticide-free brown rice is grown on the restaurant's own rice paddies and prepared with cold water from Kawachi Village; refills of rice are offered.
The Seed Lunch is the number-one seller and typically sells out roughly an hour after the doors open.

Ingredients are emphasized as organic, pesticide-free and additive-free, including brown rice from the restaurant's own paddies.

Roux-based Japanese curry is thickened with wheat flour, the cutlets are coated in wheat breadcrumbs, and items like hayashi rice and spaghetti are also wheat-based. There is no documented gluten-free menu or allergen handling. This is not a celiac-safe place.
kz_kitchen_yuki_musashi_ten.vegan_detail: The menu is built around meat: pork/chicken cutlet curries, hayashi rice and other yoshoku staples, with the curry roux and sauces typically meat-based. No documented vegetarian or vegan options. Not a vegan destination.
kz_kitchen_yuki_musashi_ten.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 11:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:00); Sun 11:00-19:00 (L.O. 18:30). Located inside Kanazawa M'ZA B1F; follows the department store's calendar.
kz_kitchen_yuki_musashi_ten.notes: Kitchen Yuki is a long-established yoshoku (Japanese Western-style) restaurant with more than 40 years of history, widely regarded as one of the roots of 'Kanazawa Curry' — the regional style of dark, glossy, thick curry served over rice and eaten with a fork or spoon, usually to

chef_bio.origin: Musashi, Kanazawa, Ishikawa (main store in Hakusan)
chef_bio.background: Kitchen Yuki is a long-established yoshoku (Japanese Western-style) restaurant tracing its roots to 1966, when founder Yukio Miyajima started out near Kanazawa Station, and it is widely regarded as one of the origins of 'Kanazawa Curry' — the regional style of dark, glossy, thick curry served over rice and eaten with a fork or spoon, usually topped with a crisp cutlet. This Musashi branch brought the storied name into the Kanazawa M'ZA department store at the Musashi crossing, a short walk from Omicho Market.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house emphasizes a long-simmered, homemade curry sauce aiming for richness and complexity rather than simple spiciness.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa black curry — a deeply colored, near-black curry prized for its rich, mellow depth rather than sharp heat. The Musashi branch is a curry-focused outlet with a narrower menu than the main store; its signature is the cutlet (tonkatsu) curry, served quickly on the classic stainless boat dish.

anecdotes.text: Kitchen Yuki is described as one of the origins of Kanazawa Curry, with a black curry sauce so dark it is nearly the color of its name.
The revered Kitchen Yuki name opened a branch inside the Kanazawa M'ZA department store (15-1 Musashi-cho), a curry-focused counter that serves its Kanazawa curry to the city center.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon記事は1966年に宮島幸雄氏が金沢駅前で創業、金沢カレーのルーツの一つ、黒いカレーを記載。tacsp記事はエムザ(武蔵町15-1)店が本店より品数が少なく金沢カレーにほぼ特化、トンカツカレーが看板、券売機で提供と確認(カマンベール/ハヤシは本記事に記載なし)。

vegan_cross_contact.text: The curry sauce and menu are meat-based (pork and chicken cutlets, hayashi rice), with no documented vegetarian or vegan preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, easy department-store-basement curry counter where you order a clearly named dish (point at the popular Kanazawa Black Katsu Curry) and pay by card or QR, so a foreign student can manage without much Japanese, but staff likely speak little English and there is no allergen support.

kz_curio_espresso_and_vinta.gf_detail: No dedicated or documented gluten-free menu. Core offerings (BBQ pork sandwiches, breakfast sandwiches, carrot cake, pastries) are wheat-based, so the kitchen is not gluten-free. A celiac traveler should not assume any item is safe; ask staff directly (English-speaking) before ordering.
kz_curio_espresso_and_vinta.vegan_detail: No documented vegan menu. The cafe centers on espresso drinks (dairy milk) plus meat/egg/cheese sandwiches and dairy/egg baked goods. Plant-milk substitution for espresso drinks is plausible at a Seattle-style cafe but is not documented, so ask. Few if any fully vegan food options.
kz_curio_espresso_and_vinta.hours_raw: 8:00-15:00; closed Tuesday and Wednesday (some listings show 9:00-18:00; current Tabelog and cafe coverage indicate 8:00-15:00 with Tue/Wed closed)
kz_curio_espresso_and_vinta.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small independent cafe opened by a Seattle native and his Japanese partner who previously worked in the Seattle coffee scene. It occupies a renovated traditional machiya townhouse at the entrance of the Yokoyasuecho shopping street (Kanazawa Omote-Sando), a short walk from Omic

chef_bio.background: A small independent cafe opened by a Seattle native and his Japanese partner who previously worked in the Seattle coffee scene. It occupies a renovated traditional machiya townhouse at the entrance of the Yokoyasuecho shopping street (Kanazawa Omote-Sando), a short walk from Omicho Market.
chef_bio.philosophy: Bring genuine Seattle specialty-coffee culture and homemade American cafe food to Kanazawa, using beans sourced from Seattle and roasted locally then blended from five varieties for depth.
chef_bio.specialty: Seattle-style espresso drinks (cinnamon latte, the coffee-jelly Crystal latte), house-made barbecue pork sandwiches on sourdough, breakfast sandwiches, and spiced carrot cake

anecdotes.text: The shop is decorated with the owners' eclectic vintage collection - antique cameras and sewing machines - and still rings up orders on a working cash register from 1943.
Beans are sourced from Seattle, roasted in Kanazawa, and blended from five varieties to build complexity in the espresso.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon記事はシアトル出身の夫とシアトルのコーヒー店で働いた日本人妻が営む、横安江町の町家改装、シアトルの豆を金沢で焙煎し5種ブレンド、1943年製レジを実使用、カメラ・ミシンの装飾、自家製BBQポークサンド/キャロットケーキを確認。

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff speak English, which makes it easier for a foreign visitor to ask about ingredients and allergens directly.

positives.text: English-speaking owners and staff at an American-style cafe make communicating dietary needs straightforward.

cultural_comfort.note: Run by a Seattle native and his Japanese partner with English-speaking staff and an American-cafe menu, so a foreign student can order entirely in English and feel at home here.

kz_cafe_yasuecho_jardin.gf_detail: The signature items are thick wheat pancakes and freshly baked scones, both made from wheat flour, so the menu is wheat-centric and not celiac-safe. No gluten-free menu or dedicated handling is documented.
kz_cafe_yasuecho_jardin.vegan_detail: Core offerings rely on dairy and eggs — pancakes and scones served with rich Hokkaido cream, and a kuzu milk pudding made with milk and cream. No vegan or plant-based options are documented.
kz_cafe_yasuecho_jardin.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yasuecho Jardin opened in 2014, tucked at the end of a narrow corridor inside Machiya5 — a mixed-use complex of design studios and IT offices set in a restored Meiji-era townhouse, just minutes from Kanazawa Station yet feeling like a step into another world. The owner, Rieko Kos

chef_bio.background: Yasuecho Jardin opened in 2014, tucked at the end of a narrow corridor inside Machiya5 — a mixed-use complex of design studios and IT offices set in a restored Meiji-era townhouse, just minutes from Kanazawa Station yet feeling like a step into another world. The owner, Rie Koishi (小紙理恵), made the bold choice to open the café at fifty rather than slow down, pouring her love of food into a small, personal space.
chef_bio.philosophy: Koishi serves only what she herself finds genuinely delicious and refuses to compromise on ingredient quality. The name 'Jardin' is French for 'garden,' reflecting the lush green view from the windows; even the lounge chairs are chosen with care (sourced from Osaka's TRUCK) for comfort and longevity, and sweets are paired with drinks to deepen the experience.
chef_bio.specialty: Freshly baked scones (about 800 yen, baked to order over ~30 minutes and served warm with rich Hokkaido cream and homemade blueberry jam), thick crisp-edged, fluffy pancakes, and a made-to-order kuzu milk pudding using traditional kuzu topped with kinako and black syrup. Coffee is made with beans sourced from a Tokyo café and extracted by cloth drip for a rich, deep flavor.

anecdotes.text: The owner readily chats with first-time visitors and happily shares dining recommendations, giving the hidden café a warm, neighborly feel.
Guests walk through narrow machiya corridors that create an 'otherworldly' transition before reaching the soft-lit room overlooking a green garden, with quiet jazz playing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: weekend-kanazawa と manpuku は、2014年開業・小紙理恵さんが50歳で開いた店・大正/明治の町家Machiya5内・約30分焼き上げのスコーン(800円)・くず牛乳プリン・東京の喫茶店の豆をネルドリップ、を確認。jardin.kanazawacity.net(公式)はジャズBGM・庭・町家の雰囲気を裏付け。

positives.text: Sweets such as scones and the kuzu milk pudding are prepared fresh to order, so the owner is closely involved in each dish and could be asked about ingredients in person.
